To fix (4)

To fix Power Analysis Check

What we found

We detected 2 potential power analyses.

Show details

We used the LLM model ‘vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8’ to check the contents of 2 paragraphs that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.

Some essential information could not be detected: sample_size, alpha_level

power_id power_type statistical_test sample_size alpha_level power effect_size effect_size_metric software
1 sensitivity other NA NA 0.8 4.6 Cohen’s d other
2 sensitivity other NA NA 0.8 4.2 Cohen’s d other
power_id text
1;2 The follow-up preregistration (AsPredicted #251092) names “pre-treatment ratings of respondents’ own conspiracy views” as the covariate for the assignment-based tests, and the main text reports that model. Table SM12.1 also reports each test with the pre-treatment three-item Kirk composite as the covariate (the composite is the baseline measure that enters the persistence and mediation models); each covariate is entered linearly, without interaction terms. In the ITT cohort, LDS shooting beliefs give b = -0.46 (95% CI [-3.30, 2.37], p = .748) with the preregistered covariate and b = -0.07 ([-2.68, 2.55], p = .961, d = -.003) with the composite; generic conspiracy beliefs give b = -3.33 ([-6.57, -0.09], p = .044) and b = -2.92 ([-5.88, 0.04], p = .053, d = -.119), respectively. The minimum detectable effect on generic conspiracy beliefs at 80% power, computed from the standard error of the assignment coefficient in the ITT cohort as (1.96 + 0.84) × SE, is 4.6 points with the preregistered covariate (SE = 1.65 points; d = 0.19; power of roughly 33% for a true effect of 2.5 points and 44% for 3 points) and 4.2 points with the composite covariate (SE = 1.51 points; d = 0.17; power roughly 38% and 51%). The computation is reproduced by the deposited R pipeline.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 9 imprecise p values out of 167 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
ps > .30 We also note that the Debunking Dialogue had no effect on support for political violence in the Kirk study, ps > .30, perhaps because it was near floor even in the control (M Debunking Dialogue = 12.1, M Information List = 9.93, M Irrelevant Dialogue = 12.0).
ps > .29 Pre-treatment ratings for the dependent variables did not differ by condition assignment (all ps > .29).
ps > .39 Given the small number of returning participants, we pool the information list and irrelevant dialogue conditions to form one control, and these two conditions did not differ on any dependent measure (all ps > .39).
ps > .28 Pre-treatment ratings for the dependent variables did not differ by condition assignment (all ps > .28).
ps > .55 We again pool the information list and irrelevant dialogue conditions to form one control; these two conditions did not differ on either dependent measure (all ps > .55).
p ≤ .05 Sig. = contrast reported as significant (p ≤ .05) in the main text.
p ≥ .060 No such pattern appears on the primary outcome (participants’ own conspiracy belief; b = -2.14, p = .43: treated returnees rated their belief 2.30 points lower than treated non-returners, p = .32, and control returnees 0.01 points lower than control non-returners, p = .99), on hidden factors or trust, on the three-item composite that enters the persistence analysis (b = -2.72, p = .153), or on any Experiment 1 outcome (all p ≥ .060; the smallest p-value is for trust in the official explanation).
p ≤ .023 In Experiment 1, the effects of the Debunking Dialogue on the follow-up outcomes are essentially unchanged by weighting (odds ratios of .55, .47, and .49; all p ≤ .023).
p > .05 Brackets show the test of the difference between conditions, with the p-value printed where p > .05. * p ≤ .05, * * p ≤ .01, * * * p < .001.

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To fix Codebook Check

What we found

  • We parsed 21 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
  • 299 of 2288 data columns (13%) are documented in a codebook; 1989 are not.
  • A codebook was found and parsed (21 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 13% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents pid, ResponseId, cond while the data has regime, test, b. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.
Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 6 codebook/README/label sources and 2288 data columns across 97 files.

A codebook was found and parsed (21 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 13% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents pid, ResponseId, cond while the data has regime, test, b. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.

Documented but Unused Variables

21 documented variables were not matched to any data column.

Variable Label Source
pid Anonymous participant code; join key to the follow-up surveys. README.md
ResponseId Qualtrics response ID; join key to the frozen LLM codings. README.md
cond Tx = Debunking Dialogue; InfoDump = Information List; DogsCats = Irrelevant Dialogue. README.md
pre_cust, post_cust Confidence (0–100) that the participant’s own conspiracy statement is true, before / after treatment. Focal outcome. README.md
pre_con, post_con “There is a cover-up or conspiracy surrounding …” (0 = definitely false, 100 = definitely true). README.md
pre_hid, post_hid Hidden / undisclosed factors behind the event, 1–10 rescaled to 0–100 by (x − 1) / 9 · 100. README.md
pre_tru, post_tru Trust in the official explanation, 1–10 rescaled to 0–100. README.md
belief LLM classification of the pre-treatment statement: YES / MAYBE / NO. Believers = YES or MAYBE. README.md
denial TRUE for Debunking Dialogue transcripts in which the model said Kirk was alive. 37 are flagged in the raw file; 3 of them are removed by earlier exclusion steps; the other 34 (27 NO / 6 MAYBE / 1 YES) are kept in the ITT analysis and excluded in the per-protocol analysis, so the ITT sample has 7 more believers (1,042 vs. 1,035). README.md
sum_ok Whether the participant said the AI’s summary of their view was accurate (“Yes”). Used only by the summary-check contrasts summary_check / imm_sumok (101 of the 1,035 per-protocol believers did not answer “Yes”: 51 Tx / 33 InfoDump / 17 DogsCats). README.md
demrep Party identification 1 = Strongly Democratic … 7 = Strongly Republican (Experiment 2: labels mapped; Experiment 1: numeric). README.md
ck0, ck1 Three-item Kirk conspiratorialness composite (VOR_06): mean of hidden factors, cover-up belief and 100 − trust, over the available items, before (t0) and after (t1) treatment. README.md
lds Conspiratorialness about the LDS church shooting at follow-up (t2): mean of the same three items asked about that event (the item names were copied from the baseline instrument). README.md
gen Generic conspiracy beliefs at follow-up: mean of the five 0–100 items. README.md
returned 1 if lds or gen is observed (Experiment 2) / 1 if the participant appears in the screened wave-3 file (Experiment 1). README.md
whoknows Experiment 1 follow-up: 1 if the participant selected only “a few powerful members of society” and/or “a few top members of the government” as who will know the truth. README.md
whoknows_alt Alternative coding reported in the main text: 1 if any of those two options or “another group not noted here” was selected. As in the robustness chunk of VOR_03 (str_detect(coalesce(whoknows, ""), ...)), a blank response is coded 0, so all 270 returnee believers enter the model (the primary whoknows coding treats a blank as missing; 264 enter). README.md
whoknows_alt_blank_na The same alternative coding with a blank response treated as missing (N = 264); sensitivity only. README.md
hidden_bin 1 if the participant answered below the midpoint (0, 1, 2) toward “the truth will be hidden from most people”. README.md
hidden_num The same item as a 0–6 scale, reversed so that 6 = “the truth will be hidden”. README.md
disc “Provided pre-score but not post-score” marks immediate dropouts. README.md

To fix Reproducibility Check

What we found

  • We assessed 34 R code files for reproducibility and ran 32 of them (each in an isolated Docker container).
  • 1 file skipped as byte-identical duplicate of another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component).
  • 17 of 34 scripts ran without error when executed.
  • Of the others, 6 did not reproduce, 10 could not run because a package or program was not available, and 1 did not finish within the time limit.
  • 55 installable dependencies detected.
  • Metacheck detected version information that can be used to install specific versions of software for the reproducibility run. We recommend retrying the reproducibility check with recorded_versions = TRUE. This will install the required R packages, if still available. As this takes a long time, this setting is not implemented on this shared server.
  • We assessed 5 Python code files for reproducibility and ran them.
  • 4 of 5 Python scripts ran without error when executed.
  • Of the others, 1 did not reproduce.
  • 3 installable Python dependencies detected.
  • 14863 statistics stored from the extracted output; 44 of 76 reported tests matched (57.9%).

Note

See the section Reproducibility Check below for the details.

To check (4)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 81 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = .054 The same pattern was observed in both experiments for closed-ended questions assessing belief that “there is a cover-up or conspiracy surrounding [the assassination event]” (0-100 scale; Trump vs control: b = -6.96, p < .001, d = .27; Trump vs information list: b = -3.20, 95% CI [-6.44, 0.04], p = .054, d = .12; Kirk vs control: b = -7.46, 95% CI [-9.55, -5.36], p < .001, d = .29; Kirk vs information list: b = -5.92, 95% CI [-8.20, -3.63], p < .001, d = .24) and belief that “there are hidden or undisclosed factors behind the reported assassination attempt against [assassination target]” (Trump vs control: b = -7.56, p < .001, d = .3; Trump vs information list: b = -4.50, 95% CI [-8.37, -0.63], p = .018, d = .17; Kirk vs control: b = -7.64, 95% CI [-10.25, -5.02], p < .001, d = .31; Kirk vs information list: b = -6.23, 95% CI [-9.07, -3.39], p < .001, d = .24).
p = .329 However, the Debunking Dialogue did not increase trust in the official explanation for the Trump assassination attempt (vs irrelevant dialogue: b = 2.43, 95% CI [-1.58, 6.45], p = .329; vs information list: b = -0.08, 95% CI [-4.53, 4.38], p = .999), perhaps because there was no clear official explanation at the time the study was run.
p = .999 However, the Debunking Dialogue did not increase trust in the official explanation for the Trump assassination attempt (vs irrelevant dialogue: b = 2.43, 95% CI [-1.58, 6.45], p = .329; vs information list: b = -0.08, 95% CI [-4.53, 4.38], p = .999), perhaps because there was no clear official explanation at the time the study was run.
p = .17 The Debunking Dialogue did increase trust in the official explanation for the Kirk assassination relative to the irrelevant dialogue (b = 5.13, 95% CI [2.29, 7.97], p < .001, d = .19; although the difference with the Informational List condition was not significant: b = 2.20, 95% CI [-0.67, 5.07], p = .17, d = .08).
ps > .30 We also note that the Debunking Dialogue had no effect on support for political violence in the Kirk study, ps > .30, perhaps because it was near floor even in the control (M Debunking Dialogue = 12.1, M Information List = 9.93, M Irrelevant Dialogue = 12.0).
p = .076 Although these events were highly partisan, and initial belief in a conspiracy theory showed partisan differences (with Republicans more strongly believing conspiracies; see SM5), we find no reliable evidence that the treatment effect differed by party (Trump: b = 1.40, 95% CI [-0.15, 2.96], p = .076; Kirk: b = -0.07, 95% CI [-1.31, 1.17], p = .91; see SM6).

p = .66 In the Trump experiment, there was no significant interaction between Debunking Dialogue and pre-treatment belief (b = 0.039, 95% CI [-0.136, 0.214], p = .66), while in the Kirk experiment the treatment was somewhat more effective for participants who initially scored higher on the conspiracy belief (b = -0.155, 95% CI [-0.300, -0.011], p = .035; see SM7).
p = .75 Among the 872 believers who returned for the follow-up (all analyzed in their assigned condition; see Methods), the pre-registered intention-to-treat analysis found no significant effect of assignment to the Kirk Debunking Dialogue (versus the pooled control conditions) on LDS conspiracy belief within the linear model (b = -0.46, 95% CI [-3.30, 2.37], p = .75, d = -.02; Figure 3C).
p = .16 Because there was some evidence that return to the follow-up was related to condition and post-treatment belief (see Methods), we also re-estimated these models weighting returning participants by the inverse of their estimated probability of returning (SM10); with these weights, the difference in generic conspiracy beliefs was smaller and no longer significant (b = -2.34, 95% CI [-5.61, 0.92], p = .16).
p = .71 The carry-forward percentage did not differ significantly by experimental arm (other popular conspiracy beliefs: interaction p = .71; LDS: interaction p = .14); when testing post hoc whether the effect of the Debunking Dialogue on belief at follow-up is mediated by immediate belief change (controlling for pre-treatment belief), we find a significant indirect effect of the Debunking Dialogue on beliefs at follow-up through immediate belief change, for both other popular conspiracy beliefs (indirect effect = -1.16 points, 95% bootstrap CI [-2.11, -0.33]) and LDS shooting beliefs (-0.78, [-1.54, -0.07]); and no significant direct (i.e., sleeper) effects of the Debunking Dialogue (b = -1.33, p = .39, and b = 0.61, p = .66, respectively; SM12).

ps > .29 Pre-treatment ratings for the dependent variables did not differ by condition assignment (all ps > .29).
p = .74 Mean confidence in treated participants’ own conspiracy beliefs in the initial experiment did not differ by whether they participated in the subsequent survey (p = .74).
p = .98 Return rates did not differ by condition (58.7% [138/235] of believers in the Debunking Dialogue condition returned, versus 59.4% [57/96] in the Information List and 57.3% [75/131] in the Irrelevant Dialogue condition; 58.1% in the two control conditions pooled, p = .98).
p = .060 Doing so finds no significant interactions for any post-treatment outcome (the closest was for trust in the official explanation, p = .060; SM10).
ps > .39 Given the small number of returning participants, we pool the information list and irrelevant dialogue conditions to form one control, and these two conditions did not differ on any dependent measure (all ps > .39).

p = .095 As preregistered, we tested for differential return across conditions: 85.7% (454/530) of believers in the Debunking Dialogue condition returned, versus 82.7% (211/255) in the Information List and 80.5% (207/257) in the Irrelevant Dialogue condition (81.6% in the two control conditions pooled; p = .095).
ps > .55 We again pool the information list and irrelevant dialogue conditions to form one control; these two conditions did not differ on either dependent measure (all ps > .55).
p = .43 As in Study 1, when predicting immediate post-treatment outcomes, the return × condition interaction was not significant when predicting participants’ own stated belief (b = -2.14, p = .43), hidden factors (b = -0.21, p = .93), or trust in the official explanation (b = 3.66, p = .152), but was significant for the cover-up item (b = -5.22, p = .022), such that treated returnees were somewhat less, and control returnees somewhat more, conspiratorial than non-returners on that item (SM10).

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 3 code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

What we found

  • We classified 231 files: 111 data, 98 code, 22 documentation.
  • We found 106 tabular data files and extracted 2288 columns from 97 of them.
  • We grouped the files into 2 study groups (ex1, ex2), plus 6 collection-level files (README/ro-crate metadata).
  • 7 files read as a table but are not a usable rectangular dataset (validation_pp.csv: 75% of columns are free text, not variables; OSF_package_2026-10-19.zip/OSF_package_2026-10-19/1_revision_pipeline/data/experiment_2_Kirk/hallucination_kirk_alive.csv: 50% of columns are free text and 69% are mostly empty – this looks like a coding worksheet, not a rectangular dataset; OSF_package_2026-10-19.zip/OSF_package_2026-10-19/2_original_analyses/experiment_2_Kirk/hallucination_kirk_alive.csv: 50% of columns are free text and 69% are mostly empty – this looks like a coding worksheet, not a rectangular dataset; disaggregated_chats.csv: 92% of columns are free text, not variables; sentence_split_CLAUDE.csv: 99% of columns are free text, not variables; sentence_split_classic_CLAUDE.csv: 99% of columns are free text, not variables; sentence_split_kirk_CLAUDE.csv: 100% of columns are free text, not variables). No columns were extracted and they were not sent to the LLM. Share the underlying data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable) with a codebook: validation_pp.csv, OSF_package_2026-10-19.zip/OSF_package_2026-10-19/1_revision_pipeline/data/experiment_2_Kirk/hallucination_kirk_alive.csv, OSF_package_2026-10-19.zip/OSF_package_2026-10-19/2_original_analyses/experiment_2_Kirk/hallucination_kirk_alive.csv, disaggregated_chats.csv, sentence_split_CLAUDE.csv, sentence_split_classic_CLAUDE.csv, sentence_split_kirk_CLAUDE.csv. We ran automated data-quality checks on 2288 columns; 466 columns have at least one potential issue (267 columns of free text that may contain personal detail; 240 columns with leading/trailing whitespace; 103 columns with inconsistent category casing; 29 columns with no observed values (entirely empty); 16 columns with numeric values stored as text; 6 columns whose name contains file-illegal characters or is excessively long). We detected demographic columns for Age, Gender, Race. 12 files are a Qualtrics survey export (1032 rows look like previews/unfinished responses to review).

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 2288 columns across 97 data files.

Issues Identified

466 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 97 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Reproducibility Check

We ran the paper’s 34 R scripts and 5 Python scripts in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script. Metacheck detected version information that can be used to install specific versions of software for the reproducibility run. We recommend retrying the reproducibility check with recorded_versions = TRUE. This will install the required R packages, if still available. As this takes a long time, this setting is not implemented on this shared server. 1 identical copy of these scripts, which other links in the paper lead to, was not run again.

21 of 39 scripts ran to the end: 7 did not reproduce, 10 could not run because a package or program was not available, and 1 did not finish within our time limit.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

Files are missing from your deposit.

  • VOR_04.2_unfolding_conspiracies_conspiracy_coding_exp_2.R reads assassination_2_cleaned.csv.

The script stops at the line that reads the file.

  1. Find the file on your computer.
  2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it.
  3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it.

A script could not open a file, but the error does not say which.

  • VOR_05_purled.R

Check every file the script reads. Make sure each one is in the deposit, and that its location is written from the top folder of the project.

A package was not installed.

  • 01_validate_pp.R: broom.helpers
  • 02_render_itt.R: broom.helpers
  • 03_itt_text_values.R: broom.helpers
  • VOR_05_unfolding_conspiracies_main_analysis_exp_2.qmd: broom.helpers
  • VOR_06_unfolding_conspiracies_recontac_exp_2.qmd: broom.helpers
  • VOR_01.3_unfolding_conspiracies_fix_chat_disaggregation.qmd: broom.helpers
  • VOR_02_unfolding_conspiracies_main_analysis_exp_1.qmd: broom.helpers
  • VOR_03_unfolding_conspiracies_just_recontact_exp_1.qmd: broom.helpers

The code loads it in a way we could not detect before running it. List every package with its version, in renv.lock (R) or requirements.txt (Python), and load each one at the top of the script with library() or import.

A package could not be installed.

  • VOR_01_unfolding_conspiracies_initial_cleanup.R needs chatlogr.
  • VOR_04.1_unfolding_conspiracies_parsing_the_dialogues_exp_2.qmd needs chatlogr.

chatlogr is not on CRAN, and your code does not say where it comes from. If it comes from GitHub or Bioconductor, install it at the top of the script, or name the command in the README, for example remotes::install_github(“user/chatlogr”) or BiocManager::install(“chatlogr”), with the version you used.

A script uses something it does not create or load itself.

  • VOR_05_switchable.R: SAMPLE

Usually the object was still in your R session from earlier work, or another script made it.

  1. Restart R (in RStudio: Session > Restart R).
  2. Run each script from top to bottom, and fix what is missing.
  3. If a script needs results of another, save them to a file in the first script and read them in the second.
  4. Load every package with library() at the top.

A script runs longer than our limit of 5 minutes.

  • VOR_01.2_unfolding_conspiracies_conspiracy_coding.R

State in the README how long each script runs. If some steps take hours, save their results (such as fitted models) to files, add those to the deposit, and let the script read them, so readers can check the rest without waiting.

File paths

21 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: fig1_data.csv to output/fig1_data.csv (in 07_figures.R); coding__full_classic_complete.csv to ../../data/experiment_1_and_2_argument_coding/coding__full_classic_complete.csv (in 07_figures.R); coding__full_complete.csv to ../../data/experiment_1_and_2_argument_coding/coding__full_complete.csv (in 07_figures.R); coding__full_kirk_complete.csv to ../../data/experiment_1_and_2_argument_coding/coding__full_kirk_complete.csv (in 07_figures.R); fig3_trump.csv to output/fig3_trump.csv (in 07_figures.R); fig3_kirk.csv to output/fig3_kirk.csv (in 07_figures.R); fig3_annotations.csv to output/fig3_annotations.csv (in 07_figures.R); Charlie Kirk assassination_September 18, 2025_09.22.csv to ../../../data/experiment_2_Kirk/Charlie Kirk assassination_September 18, 2025_09.22.csv (in VOR_05_switchable.R); hallucination_kirk_alive.csv to ../../../data/experiment_2_Kirk/hallucination_kirk_alive.csv (in VOR_05_switchable.R); assassination_2_GPT_conspiracy_coding.csv to ../../../data/experiment_2_Kirk/assassination_2_GPT_conspiracy_coding.csv (in VOR_05_switchable.R), and 11 more. The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. The code reads files that are only inside OSF_package_2026-10-19.zip, and no script unpacks it. We unpacked it in its folder before the run. So that others can run the code as deposited, start the code with a line that unpacks it (such as unzip("OSF_package_2026-10-19.zip") in R), or upload the files unpacked. 4 data paths were built at runtime with sprintf()/paste()/file.path() instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author’s own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.

Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 1 data file that is not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: assassination_2_cleaned.csv.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 34 scripts: 17 ran without error, 14 errored, 1 timed out, 2 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 2 scripts use an object or function that only another script defines, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: VOR_01.3_unfolding_conspiracies_fix_chat_disaggregation.qmd after VOR_02_unfolding_conspiracies_main_analysis_exp_1.qmd; VOR_05_switchable.R after common.R. Such a script should source() the other itself, since it does not run on its own.

a script hit an object '...' not found error, indicating it expected a variable another script defines. We inferred which script supplies it and re-ordered so that script runs first, and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.

Undefined-variable errors

1 script failed on an undefined variable or function (object '...' not found / could not find function "..."). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper’s own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

File Missing variable Defined in
VOR_05_switchable.R SAMPLE (not defined anywhere in the paper’s code)

Dependency-unavailable errors

2 scripts could not run because their own dependency is unavailable — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so it does not force the traffic light red.

VOR_01_unfolding_conspiracies_initial_cleanup.R

setwd() in the code

3 scripts call setwd(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring a setwd() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

Reproducible after removing setwd(): common.R, VOR_07_assassination_attempt_LLM_argument_coding.qmd.

Calls that install packages in the code

1 call to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like was replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

>   for (oc in names(OUTS)) {
>     pre <- OUTS[[oc]][1]; post <- OUTS[[oc]][2]
>     # VOR_02/VOR_05 backfill: a participant is an immediate dropout iff
>     # PostCustomRating_1 is missing; dropouts get their pre-treatment value on
>     # every outcome, completers keep their observed post value (one Trump
>     # Information-List completer skipped the post trust item and is dropped
>     # from that model only).
>     d <- ds %>% filter(!is.na(.data[[pre]])) %>%

>              diff = y - .data[[pre]],
>              Condition = factor(cond, levels = c("DogsCats", "InfoDump", "Tx"))) %>%
>       filter(!is.na(y))
>     m  <- lmr(y ~ Condition + pre_c, d)
>     em <- emmeans(m, ~ Condition, data = d)
>     pw <- as.data.frame(summary(pairs(em, adjust = "tukey"), infer = c(TRUE, TRUE)))
>     tukey_rows[[length(tukey_rows) + 1]] <<- tibble(
>       sample = label, outcome = oc, contrast = as.character(pw$contrast),
>       estimate = pw$estimate, SE = pw$SE, df = pw$df, lower.CL = pw$lower.CL,
>       upper.CL = pw$upper.CL, t.ratio = pw$t.ratio, p.tukey = pw$p.value, n = nrow(d))
>     # difference-score EMMs (Figure 1 quantities)
>     md <- lmr(diff ~ Condition + pre_c, d)
>     e2 <- as.data.frame(emmeans(md, ~ Condition, data = d))
>     emm_rows[[length(emm_rows) + 1]] <<- tibble(
>       sample = label, outcome = oc, Condition = as.character(e2$Condition),
>       emmean_diff = e2$emmean, SE = e2$SE, lo95 = e2$emmean - 1.96 * e2$SE,
>       hi95 = e2$emmean + 1.96 * e2$SE, n = nrow(d))
>   }
> }

>     pre <- OUTS[[oc]][1]; post <- OUTS[[oc]][2]
>     cc <- ds %>% filter(!is.na(.data[[pre]]))
>     prem <- mean(cc[[pre]])
>     cc <- cc %>% mutate(y = ifelse(is.na(.data[[post]]), .data[[pre]], .data[[post]]),
>                         pc = .data[[pre]] - prem)
>     for (ctl in CTLS) {
>       sub <- cc %>% filter(cond %in% c("Tx", ctl)) %>% mutate(tx = as.numeric(cond == "Tx"))
>       m <- lmr(y ~ tx + pc, sub)
>       pre_sd <- sd(ds[[pre]][ds$cond %in% c("Tx", ctl) & !is.na(ds[[pre]])])
>       t <- term_lmr(m, "tx")
>       out[[paste0(oc, "_vs_", ctl)]] <- c(t, list(n = nrow(sub), d = t$b / pre_sd))
>     }
>   }
>   out
> }

> IMM_KEYS <- unlist(lapply(names(OUTS), function(oc) paste0(oc, "_vs_", CTLS)))
> dppc2 <- function(ds, ctl, pre, post) {
>   grp <- function(a) {
>     gg <- ds[ds$cond %in% a, ]
>     y  <- ifelse(is.na(gg$post_cust), gg[[pre]], gg[[post]])
>     list(n = nrow(gg), pre_m = mean(gg[[pre]], na.rm = TRUE), pre_sd = sd(gg[[pre]], na.rm = TRUE),
>          post_m = mean(y, na.rm = TRUE))
>   }
>   tx <- grp("Tx"); ct <- grp(ctl)
>   mdf <- tx$n + ct$n - 2
>   sd_pooled <- sqrt(((tx$n - 1) * tx$pre_sd^2 + (ct$n - 1) * ct$pre_sd^2) / mdf)
>   cm <- exp(lgamma(mdf / 2) - log(sqrt(mdf / 2)) - lgamma((mdf - 1) / 2))
>   cm * ((tx$post_m - tx$pre_m) - (ct$post_m - ct$pre_m)) / sd_pooled
> }
> imm3_contrasts <- function(ds) {
>   out <- list()
>   for (oc in names(OUTS)) {
>     pre <- OUTS[[oc]][1]; post <- OUTS[[oc]][2]
>     cc <- ds %>% filter(!is.na(.data[[pre]]), cond %in% ARMS)
>     prem <- mean(cc[[pre]])
>     cc <- cc %>% mutate(y = ifelse(is.na(.data[[post]]), .data[[pre]], .data[[post]]),
>                         pc = .data[[pre]] - prem,
>                         InfoDump = as.numeric(cond == "InfoDump"),
>                         DogsCats = as.numeric(cond == "DogsCats"))
>     m <- lmr(y ~ InfoDump + DogsCats + pc, cc)
>     s <- summary(m)$coefficients
>     for (ctl in CTLS) {
>       t <- term_lmr(m, ctl)
>       p_tukey <- ptukey(abs(s[ctl, "t value"]) * sqrt(2), nmeans = 3, df = s[ctl, "DF"],
>                         lower.tail = FALSE)
>       half <- unname(qtukey(0.95, nmeans = 3, df = s[ctl, "DF"]) / sqrt(2) * s[ctl, "Std. Error"])
>       out[[paste0(oc, "_vs_", ctl)]] <- list(b = -t$b, lo = -t$hi, hi = -t$lo, p = t$p,
>                                             p_tukey = unname(p_tukey), n = nrow(cc),
>                                             lo_tukey = -t$b - half, hi_tukey = -t$b + half,
>                                             d = dppc2(ds, ctl, pre, post))
>     }
>   }
>   out
> }

==== 03_followup ====
> RES <- load_results()
> CO <- load_cohorts()
> followup_block <- function(ds) {
>   an <- ds %>% filter(returned == 1 & cond %in% ARMS) %>%
>     mutate(tx = as.numeric(cond == "Tx"))
>   out <- list(n = nrow(an), arms = arm_counts(an$cond))
>   for (oc in c("lds", "gen")) {
>     cc <- an %>% filter(!is.na(.data[[oc]]) & !is.na(ck0)) %>% mutate(y = .data[[oc]])
>     m  <- lmr(y ~ tx + ck0, cc)
>     t  <- term_lmr(m, "tx")
>     out[[paste0("anc_", oc)]] <- c(t, list(d = t$b / sd(cc$y), n = nrow(cc)))
>     cc2 <- an %>% filter(!is.na(.data[[oc]]) & !is.na(pre_cust)) %>% mutate(y = .data[[oc]])
>     # preregistered covariate; d = b / SD of the outcome among this model's rows,
>     # as for anc_<oc> above
>     t2 <- term_lmr(lmr(y ~ tx + pre_cust, cc2), "tx")
>     out[[paste0("anc_", oc, "_precust")]] <- c(t2, list(d = t2$b / sd(cc2$y), n = nrow(cc2)))
>     # Lin persistence: d2 = t2 - t0 on d1 = t1 - t0 and t0 (classical OLS)
>     cc3 <- cc %>% filter(!is.na(ck1)) %>% mutate(d2 = y - ck0, d1 = ck1 - ck0, t0 = ck0)
>     out[[paste0("lin_", oc)]] <- c(term_lm(lm(d2 ~ d1 + t0, cc3), "d1"), list(n = nrow(cc3)))
>     for (grp in c(tx = 1, ctl = 0)) {
>       gg <- cc3 %>% filter(tx == grp)
>       out[[paste0("lin_", oc, "_", names(which(c(tx = 1, ctl = 0) == grp)))]] <-
>         c(term_lm(lm(d2 ~ d1 + t0, gg), "d1"), list(n = nrow(gg)))
>     }
>     out[[paste0("lin_", oc, "_int")]] <- term_lm(lm(d2 ~ d1 + t0 + tx + d1:tx, cc3), "d1:tx")
>     # worst-case return imputation over all believers with t0 and t1
>     base <- ds %>% filter(cond %in% ARMS & !is.na(ck0) & !is.na(ck1)) %>%
>       mutate(d2 = ifelse(returned == 1 & !is.na(.data[[oc]]), .data[[oc]] - ck0, 0),
>              d1 = ck1 - ck0, t0 = ck0)
>     out[[paste0("lin_", oc, "_imputed")]] <- c(term_lm(lm(d2 ~ d1 + t0, base), "d1"), list(n = nrow(base)))
>     # Lin persistence with the own-belief rating as t0/t1 (SI sensitivity row): (t2 - pre_cust) ~ (post_cust - pre_cust) + pre_cust, classical
>     # OLS, rows with the outcome, pre_cust and post_cust observed (851 ITT / 845 PP)
>     cc4 <- an %>% filter(!is.na(.data[[oc]]) & !is.na(pre_cust) & !is.na(post_cust)) %>%
>       mutate(d2 = .data[[oc]] - pre_cust, d1 = post_cust - pre_cust, t0 = pre_cust)
>     out[[paste0("lin_", oc, "_precust")]] <- c(term_lm(lm(d2 ~ d1 + t0, cc4), "d1"), list(n = nrow(cc4)))
>   }
>   # SE-based sensitivity (minimum detectable effect, power) of the assignment-based tests:
>   # SE from the HC2 95% CI; MDE at 80% power (two-sided alpha .05) = (1.96 + 0.84) x SE;
>   # power for a true effect of 2.5 and 3.0 points = P(|Z| > 1.96 | mean = effect / SE)
>   z_a <- qnorm(0.975); z_b <- qnorm(0.80)
>   for (oc in c("lds", "gen")) {
>     sd_y <- out[[paste0("anc_", oc)]]$b / out[[paste0("anc_", oc)]]$d
>     for (key in c(paste0("anc_", oc), paste0("anc_", oc, "_precust"))) {
>       a <- out[[key]]; se <- (a$hi - a$lo) / (2 * z_a); mde <- (z_a + z_b) * se
>       out[[paste0(key, "_power")]] <- list(
>         se = se, mde80 = mde, mde80_d = mde / sd_y,
>         power_2_5 = pnorm(z_a - 2.5 / se, lower.tail = FALSE) + pnorm(-z_a - 2.5 / se),
>         power_3_0 = pnorm(z_a - 3.0 / se, lower.tail = FALSE) + pnorm(-z_a - 3.0 / se))
>     }
>   }
>   # differential return among all believers in ds
>   tx_n <- sum(ds$cond == "Tx"); tx_r <- sum(ds$returned[ds$cond == "Tx"])
>   ct_n <- sum(ds$cond != "Tx"); ct_r <- sum(ds$returned[ds$cond != "Tx"])
>   ct <- chisq.test(matrix(c(tx_r, tx_n - tx_r, ct_r, ct_n - ct_r), 2, byrow = TRUE), correct = TRUE)
>   out$return_rates <- list(tx = tx_r / tx_n, ctl = ct_r / ct_n, tx_n = tx_n, ctl_n = ct_n,
>                            p = unname(ct$p.value))
>   # return by randomized condition (three arms) + 2 x 3 chi-square, no continuity correction
>   out$return_by_cond <- return_by_cond(ds)
>   out
> }

> tf_model <- function(key, binary = TRUE) {

>     m <- glm(y ~ tx + pc, data = cc, family = binomial)
>     t <- term_glm(m, "tx")
>     # lo/hi: Wald CI (as in r2_battery.py); lo_prof/hi_prof: profile-likelihood

>     list(or_ = exp(t$b), lo = exp(t$lo), hi = exp(t$hi), p = t$p, n = nrow(cc),

>   } else c(term_lmr(lmr(y ~ tx + pc, cc), "tx"), list(n = nrow(cc)))
> }

>     res$ret_eff_ctl <- term_lmr(lmr(y ~ ret + pc, cc %>% filter(tx == 0)), "ret")

>   if (composite) {

>   out
> }

> rename_by_number <- function(df, prefix, number_mapping) {
>   # Find columns that match the pattern: prefix followed by a number
>   pattern <- paste0("^", prefix, "_([0-9]+)$")
>   cols_to_rename <- names(df)[grepl(pattern, names(df))]
>   
>   # For each column that matches the pattern
>   for (col in cols_to_rename) {
>     # Extract the number part
>     number <- gsub(pattern, "\\1", col)
>     
>     # If this number exists in our mapping
>     if (number %in% names(number_mapping)) {
>       # Create the new name
>       new_name <- paste0(prefix, "_", number_mapping[number])
>       
>       # Rename the column
>       names(df)[names(df) == col] <- new_name
>     }
>   }
>   
>   return(df)
> }

> calculate_dppc2 <- function(data, pre_col, post_col, group_col) {
>   # Summarize data by group
>   summary_stats <- data %>%
>     group_by({{ group_col }}) %>%
>     summarise(
>       pre_mean = mean({{ pre_col }}, na.rm = TRUE),
>       pre_sd = sd({{ pre_col }}, na.rm = TRUE),
>       post_mean = mean({{ post_col }}, na.rm = TRUE),
>       post_sd = sd({{ post_col }}, na.rm = TRUE),
>       n = n(),
>       .groups = 'drop'
>     )
>   
>   # Extract treatment and control stats
>   T.n <- summary_stats[2, ]$n
>   C.n <- summary_stats[1, ]$n
>   
>   T.sd_pre <- summary_stats[2, ]$pre_sd
>   C.sd_pre <- summary_stats[1, ]$pre_sd
>   
>   T.m_post <- summary_stats[2, ]$post_mean
>   C.m_post <- summary_stats[1, ]$post_mean
>   
>   T.m_pre <- summary_stats[2, ]$pre_mean
>   C.m_pre <- summary_stats[1, ]$pre_mean
>   
>   # Calculate pooled standard deviation
>   sd.pooled <- sqrt(((T.n - 1) * T.sd_pre^2 + (C.n - 1) * C.sd_pre^2) / (T.n + C.n - 2))
>   
>   # Calculate the effect size using Cohen's method
>   yi <- metafor:::.cmicalc(T.n + C.n - 2) * ((T.m_post - T.m_pre) - (C.m_post - C.m_pre)) / sd.pooled
>   
>   # Return a list containing all computed values
>   list(
>     treatment_n = T.n,
>     control_n = C.n,
>     treatment_pre_sd = round(T.sd_pre, 2),
>     control_pre_sd = round(C.sd_pre, 2),
>     treatment_post_mean = round(T.m_post, 2),
>     control_post_mean = round(C.m_post, 2),
>     treatment_pre_mean = round(T.m_pre, 2),
>     control_pre_mean = round(C.m_pre, 2),
>     pooled_sd = round(sd.pooled, 2),
>     effect_size = round(yi, 2)
>   )
> }
> calculate_d_postonly <- function(data, outcome_col, group_col) {
>   # Summarize data by group
>   summary_stats <- data %>%
>     group_by({{ group_col }}) %>%
>     summarise(
>       mean = mean({{ outcome_col }}, na.rm = TRUE),
>       sd = sd({{ outcome_col }}, na.rm = TRUE),
>       n = n(),
>       .groups = 'drop'
>     )
>   
>   # Extract treatment and control stats
>   T.n <- summary_stats[2, ]$n
>   C.n <- summary_stats[1, ]$n
>   
>   T.mean <- summary_stats[2, ]$mean
>   C.mean <- summary_stats[1, ]$mean
>   
>   T.sd <- summary_stats[2, ]$sd
>   C.sd <- summary_stats[1, ]$sd
>   
>   # Calculate pooled standard deviation
>   sd.pooled <- sqrt(((T.n - 1) * T.sd^2 + (C.n - 1) * C.sd^2) / (T.n + C.n - 2))
>   
>   # Calculate Cohen's d with bias correction
>   d <- metafor:::.cmicalc(T.n + C.n - 2) * (T.mean - C.mean) / sd.pooled
>   
>   # Return results
>   list(
>     treatment_n = T.n,
>     control_n = C.n,
>     treatment_mean = round(T.mean, 2),
>     control_mean = round(C.mean, 2),
>     treatment_sd = round(T.sd, 2),
>     control_sd = round(C.sd, 2),
>     pooled_sd = round(sd.pooled, 2),
>     cohens_d = round(d, 2)
>   )
> }

==== 05_lee_bounds ====
> RES <- load_results()
> CO <- load_cohorts()
> NBOOT <- 2000
> set.seed(SEED)
> sd0 <- function(x) { x <- x[!is.na(x)]; sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2)) }
> lee_bounds <- function(cond, y, ctl) {
>   is_tx <- cond == "Tx"
>   t_obs <- y[is_tx & !is.na(y)]; c_obs <- y[!is_tx & !is.na(y)]
>   pt <- length(t_obs) / sum(is_tx); pc <- length(c_obs) / sum(!is_tx)
>   if (pt >= pc) {
>     trim <- sort(t_obs); other <- c_obs; tp <- 1 - pc / pt
>     k <- as.integer(round(length(trim) * tp)); n <- length(trim)
>     hi_t <- mean(trim[(k + 1):n]) - mean(other)
>     lo_t <- mean(trim[1:(n - k)]) - mean(other)
>   } else {
>     trim <- sort(c_obs); other <- t_obs; tp <- 1 - pt / pc
>     k <- as.integer(round(length(trim) * tp)); n <- length(trim)
>     hi_t <- mean(other) - mean(trim[1:(n - k)])
>     lo_t <- mean(other) - mean(trim[(k + 1):n])
>   }
>   c(lo = min(lo_t, hi_t), hi = max(lo_t, hi_t), pt = pt, pc = pc, tp = tp)
> }
> lee <- function(ds, ctl, pre, post, nboot = NBOOT) {
>   sub <- ds %>% filter(cond %in% c("Tx", ctl) & !is.na(.data[[pre]]))
>   cond <- sub$cond; y <- sub[[post]]
>   b <- lee_bounds(cond, y, ctl)
>   naive <- mean(y[cond == "Tx"], na.rm = TRUE) - mean(y[cond == ctl], na.rm = TRUE)
>   bl <- bu <- rep(NA_real_, nboot); n <- nrow(sub)
>   for (i in seq_len(nboot)) {
>     idx <- sample.int(n, n, replace = TRUE)
>     r <- tryCatch(lee_bounds(cond[idx], y[idx], ctl), error = function(e) c(lo = NA, hi = NA))
>     bl[i] <- r[["lo"]]; bu[i] <- r[["hi"]]
>   }
>   list(lo = unname(b["lo"]), hi = unname(b["hi"]), naive = naive,
>        rate_tx = unname(b["pt"]), rate_ctl = unname(b["pc"]), trim = unname(b["tp"]),
>        trimmed_arm = if (b["pt"] >= b["pc"]) "Tx" else ctl,
>        ci_lo = unname(b["lo"] - 1.96 * sd0(bl)), ci_hi = unname(b["hi"] + 1.96 * sd0(bu)),
>        n_tx = sum(cond == "Tx"), n_ctl = sum(cond == ctl),
>        boot_sd_lo = sd0(bl), boot_sd_hi = sd0(bu), nboot = nboot, seed = SEED)
> }
> RES$lee <- list()
> rows <- list()

> split_llm_sentences <- function(text) {
>   if (is.na(text) || nchar(text) == 0) return(character(0))
>   
>   # Fix encoding
>   clean <- str_replace_all(text, '‚Äì', '—')
>   clean <- str_replace_all(clean, '‚Äú', '"')
>   clean <- str_replace_all(clean, '‚Äù', '"')
>   clean <- str_replace_all(clean, '‚Äô', "'")
>   
>   # Remove markdown
>   clean <- str_replace_all(clean, "\\*\\*", "")
>   clean <- str_replace_all(clean, "\\* ", "")
>   
>   # Split on paragraph/turn delimiters
>   clean <- str_replace_all(clean, "([.!?:])nn([A-Z*])", "\\1|||PARA|||\\2")
>   clean <- str_replace_all(clean, "([.!?])\\s+nn([A-Z])", "\\1|||PARA|||\\2")
>   clean <- str_replace_all(clean, " n\\* ", "|||PARA|||")
>   clean <- str_replace_all(clean, "([.!?:]) n([A-Z*])", "\\1|||PARA|||\\2")
>   clean <- str_replace_all(clean, "([.!?:])n([A-Z])", "\\1|||PARA|||\\2")
>   clean <- str_replace_all(clean, " n$", "|||PARA|||")
>   
>   # Split into paragraphs
>   paragraphs <- str_split(clean, "\\|\\|\\|PARA\\|\\|\\|")[[1]]
>   paragraphs <- str_trim(paragraphs)
>   paragraphs <- paragraphs[nzchar(paragraphs)]
>   
>   # Split each paragraph into sentences
>   sentences <- map(paragraphs, function(para) {
>     sents <- str_split(para, "(?<=[.!?])\\s+(?=[A-Z])")[[1]]
>     sents <- str_trim(sents)
>     sents[nzchar(sents)]
>   })
>   
>   sentences <- unlist(sentences)
>   
>   # NEW: Clean up any remaining stray " n " patterns
>   # After splitting, replace any " n " that's left (these are just spaces)
>   sentences <- str_replace_all(sentences, " n ", " ")
>   
>   # Also catch " n" at end of sentences
>   sentences <- str_replace_all(sentences, " n([.!?])$", "\\1")
>   
>   return(sentences)
> }

> categorize_parallel_advanced <- function(data,
>                                          column,
>                                          system_prompt,
>                                          categories,
>                                          context_columns = NULL,
>                                          include_reasoning = TRUE,
>                                          include_confidence = TRUE,
>                                          provider = "openai",

>                                          progress_update_interval = 0.5) {
>   
>   # Check for required packages
>   for (pkg in c("future", "furrr", "progressr")) {
>     if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
>       stop(paste0("Package '", pkg, "' is required for advanced parallelization. ",
>                   "Please install it with invisible(NULL)"))
>     }
>   }
>   
>   # Input validation
>   if (!is.data.frame(data)) {
>     stop("'data' must be a data frame or tibble")
>   }
>   
>   # Handle column input
>   if (is.character(column)) {
>     if (!column %in% names(data)) {
>       stop(paste0("Column '", column, "' not found in data"))
>     }
>     col_name <- column
>   } else if (is.numeric(column)) {
>     if (column > ncol(data)) {
>       stop(paste0("Column index ", column, " exceeds number of columns in data"))
>     }
>     col_name <- names(data)[column]
>   } else {
>     stop("'column' must be a column name or index")
>   }
>   
>   # Extract the column to categorize
>   texts <- data[[col_name]]
>   n <- length(texts)
>   
>   # Extract context columns if provided
>   context_data <- NULL
>   if (!is.null(context_columns)) {
>     # Validate context columns exist
>     missing_cols <- setdiff(context_columns, names(data))
>     if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
>       stop(paste0("Context columns not found in data: ", paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", ")))
>     }
>     # Extract context as a list of vectors
>     context_data <- lapply(context_columns, function(col) data[[col]])
>     names(context_data) <- context_columns
>   }
>   
>   # Set up the type schema for structured data extraction
>   if (include_reasoning && include_confidence) {
>     type <- ellmer::type_object(
>       category = ellmer::type_string(
>         description = paste0("The category for the text, one of: ", paste(categories, collapse = ", "))
>       ),
>       confidence = ellmer::type_number(
>         description = "Confidence score between 0 and 1, with 1 being most confident",
>       ),
>       reasoning = ellmer::type_string(
>         description = "Brief explanation of why this category was chosen"
>       )
>     )
>   } else if (include_reasoning) {
>     type <- ellmer::type_object(
>       category = ellmer::type_string(
>         description = paste0("The category for the text, one of: ", paste(categories, collapse = ", "))
>       ),
>       reasoning = ellmer::type_string(
>         description = "Brief explanation of why this category was chosen"
>       )
>     )
>   } else if (include_confidence) {
>     type <- ellmer::type_object(
>       category = ellmer::type_string(
>         description = paste0("The category for the text, one of: ", paste(categories, collapse = ", "))
>       ),
>       confidence = ellmer::type_number(
>         description = "Confidence score between 0 and 1, with 1 being most confident",
>       )
>     )
>   } else {
>     type <- ellmer::type_object(
>       category = ellmer::type_string(
>         description = paste0("The category for the text, one of: ", paste(categories, collapse = ", "))
>       )
>     )
>   }
>   
>   # Initialize the parallelization strategy
>   future::plan(parallel_strategy, workers = workers)
>   
>   # Configure progress reporting
>   if (echo != "none") {
>     if (show_progress) {
>       # Create a progress bar
>       progressr::handlers(progressr::handler_progress(
>         format = "[:bar] :percent | Items: :current/:total | Elapsed: :elapsed | ETA: :eta",
>         clear = FALSE,
>         width = 80,

>       ))
>     } else {

>   }
>   
>   # Split texts into chunks for processing
>   chunks <- split(seq_along(texts), ceiling(seq_along(texts) / chunk_size))
>   
>   # Define the worker function with all parameters explicitly passed
>   process_chunk <- function(indices, p, texts, system_prompt, provider, model, 
>                            temperature, context_data, categories, 
>                            include_reasoning, include_confidence, 
>                            rate_limit_per_minute, echo, type) {
>     # Set up a new chat instance
>     provider_fn <- eval(parse(text = paste0("ellmer::chat_", provider)))
>     chat_args <- list(system_prompt = system_prompt, echo = "none")
>     if (!is.null(model)) chat_args$model <- model
>     
>     # Pass temperature through api_args
>     if (!is.null(temperature)) {
>       chat_args$api_args <- list(temperature = temperature)
>     }
>     
>     chat <- do.call(provider_fn, chat_args)
>     
>     # Process each item in the chunk
>     results <- vector("list", length(indices))
>     
>     # Create a throttle mechanism for rate limiting
>     last_call_time <- Sys.time() - 1
>     min_interval <- 60 / rate_limit_per_minute
>     chunk_start_time <- Sys.time()
>     
>     for (i in seq_along(indices)) {
>       idx <- indices[i]
>       
>       # Rate limiting with adaptive wait
>       if (i > 1 && rate_limit_per_minute < 600) {
>         elapsed <- as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), last_call_time, units = "secs"))
>         if (elapsed < min_interval) {
>           Sys.sleep(min_interval - elapsed)
>         }
>       }
>       last_call_time <- Sys.time()
>       
>       # Update progress for each item
>       if (echo != "none") {
>         p(amount = 1, message = sprintf("Item %d", idx))
>       }
>       
>       # Create prompt with context
>       text <- texts[idx]
>       
>       # Build prompt with context sentences
>       prompt_parts <- c()
>       
>       # Add context sentences if available

>           context_value <- context_data[[col_name]][idx]

>             prompt_parts <- c(prompt_parts, 
>                             paste0("Context (", col_name, "): \"", context_value, "\""))
>           }
>         }
>         if (length(prompt_parts) > 0) {
>           prompt_parts <- c(prompt_parts, "")  # Add blank line
>         }
>       }
>       
>       # Add the main target sentence
>       prompt_parts <- c(prompt_parts,
>                        paste0("Target sentence to analyze:\n\"", text, "\""))
>       
>       # Combine into full prompt
>       prompt <- paste0(paste(prompt_parts, collapse = "\n\n"),
>                       "\n\nCategorize this target sentence as: ", 
>                       paste(categories, collapse = ", "), ".")
>       
>       if (include_reasoning) {

>       }
>       
>       if (include_confidence) {
>         prompt <- paste0(prompt, " Also provide your confidence level (0-1) in this categorization.")
>       }
>       
>       # Handle potential errors
>       tryCatch({
>         results[[i]] <- chat$extract_data(prompt, type = type)
>       }, error = function(e) {
>         empty_result <- list(category = NA_character_)
>         if (include_confidence) empty_result$confidence <- NA_real_
>         if (include_reasoning) empty_result$reasoning <- NA_character_
>         results[[i]] <- empty_result
>       })
>     }
>     
>     return(results)
>   }
>   
>   # Run the parallel processing with improved progress reporting
>   progressr::with_progress({
>     # Create a progressor that tracks overall items rather than chunks
>     p <- progressr::progressor(steps = n)
>     
>     # Use future_map to process chunks in parallel
>     results_by_chunk <- furrr::future_map(
>       chunks, 
>       function(indices) {
>         result <- process_chunk(
>           indices = indices, 
>           p = p,
>           texts = texts,
>           system_prompt = system_prompt,
>           provider = provider,
>           model = model,
>           temperature = temperature,
>           context_data = context_data,
>           categories = categories,
>           include_reasoning = include_reasoning,
>           include_confidence = include_confidence,
>           rate_limit_per_minute = rate_limit_per_minute,
>           echo = echo,
>           type = type
>         )
>         return(result)
>       },
>       .options = furrr::furrr_options(seed = TRUE)
>     )
>   }, handlers = if(echo != "none") {
>     progressr::handler_progress(
>       format = "[:bar] :percent | Items: :current/:total | Elapsed: :elapsed | ETA: :eta",
>       clear = FALSE,
>       width = 80
>     )
>   })
>   
>   # Flatten the results
>   results <- unlist(results_by_chunk, recursive = FALSE)
>   
>   # Make sure results are in the correct order
>   results <- results[order(unlist(chunks))]
>   
>   # Add the results to the original data
>   data$category <- sapply(results, function(r) r$category)
>   
>   if (include_confidence) {
>     data$confidence <- sapply(results, function(r) r$confidence)
>   }
>   
>   if (include_reasoning) {
>     data$reasoning <- sapply(results, function(r) r$reasoning)
>   }
>   
>   # Return to sequential mode
>   future::plan(future::sequential)
>   
>   return(data)
> }
> extract_categories <- function(category_string) {
>   if (is.na(category_string)) return(integer(0))
>   numbers <- str_extract_all(category_string, "\\b[1-8]\\b")[[1]]
>   unique(as.integer(numbers))
> }
> calculate_llm_human_agreement <- function(llm_col, human_col, strategy_name) {
>   complete_cases <- !is.na(llm_col) & !is.na(human_col)
>   llm_clean <- llm_col[complete_cases]
>   human_clean <- human_col[complete_cases]
>   
>   pct_agree <- mean(llm_clean == human_clean) * 100
>   kappa_val <- kappa2(data.frame(llm_clean, human_clean))$value
>   
>   n_total <- length(llm_clean)
>   both_yes <- sum(llm_clean == 1 & human_clean == 1)
>   llm_yes_human_no <- sum(llm_clean == 1 & human_clean == 0)
>   llm_no_human_yes <- sum(llm_clean == 0 & human_clean == 1)
>   both_no <- sum(llm_clean == 0 & human_clean == 0)
>   
>   precision <- ifelse((both_yes + llm_yes_human_no) > 0,
>                       both_yes / (both_yes + llm_yes_human_no), NA_real_)
>   recall    <- ifelse((both_yes + llm_no_human_yes) > 0,
>                       both_yes / (both_yes + llm_no_human_yes), NA_real_)
>   f1        <- ifelse(!is.na(precision) & !is.na(recall) & (precision + recall) > 0,
>                       2 * (precision * recall) / (precision + recall), NA_real_)
>   
>   tibble(
>     strategy = strategy_name,
>     n = n_total,
>     pct_agreement = pct_agree,
>     kappa = kappa_val,
>     precision = precision,
>     recall = recall,
>     f1 = f1,
>     both_yes_pct = both_yes / n_total * 100,
>     llm_yes_human_no_pct = llm_yes_human_no / n_total * 100,
>     llm_no_human_yes_pct = llm_no_human_yes / n_total * 100,
>     both_no_pct = both_no / n_total * 100
>   )
> }

> create_category_table <- function(data, category_col, category_name, n = 10) {
>   
>   examples <- data %>%
>     filter(!!sym(category_col) == 1) %>%
>     dplyr::select(identifier, target_sentence, sentence_minus1, sentence_minus2) %>%
>     head(n) %>%
>     mutate(
>       example_num = row_number(),
>       # Create context column combining -2 and -1
>       context = case_when(
>         !is.na(sentence_minus2) & !is.na(sentence_minus1) ~ 
>           paste0(sentence_minus2, " | ", sentence_minus1),
>         !is.na(sentence_minus1) ~ sentence_minus1,
>         !is.na(sentence_minus2) ~ sentence_minus2,
>         TRUE ~ ""
>       )
>     ) %>%
>     dplyr::select(example_num, context, target_sentence)
>   
>   n_found <- sum(data[[category_col]] == 1, na.rm = TRUE)
>   
>   # Create table
>   cat("\n### ", category_name, " (n = ", n_found, ")\n\n", sep = "")
>   
>   if (nrow(examples) > 0) {
>     tbl <- kable(examples,
>                  col.names = c("#", "Context", "Target Sentence"),
>                  caption = paste0(category_name, " (", n_found, " total examples)")) %>%
>       kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
>     print(tbl)
>   } else {
>     cat("No examples found for this category.\n")
>   }
>   
>   cat("\n")
>   
>   return(invisible(examples))
> }
> cat("\n\n")

> label_strategy <- function(df) {
>   df %>%
>     mutate(
>       strategy_clean = case_when(
>         strategy == "rational_persuasion" ~ "Rational Persuasion",

>         strategy == "building_rapport" ~ "Building Rapport",
>         strategy == "emphasizing_unknowns" ~ "Epistemic Humility",
>         strategy == "highlighting_harms" ~ "Highlight Harms",
>         strategy == "socratic_questioning" ~ "Socratic Questioning",

>         strategy == "none_of_these" ~ "None of These"
>       )
>     )
> }
> strategy_vars <- c("rational_persuasion", "stories_metaphors", "building_rapport", 
>                    "emphasizing_unknowns", "highlighting_harms", "socratic_questioning", 
>                    "credible_sources", "none_of_these")

> full_means <- coding__full_complete %>%

> convo_results <- function(df_a, df_b, name_b) {
>   map_df(strategy_vars, function(strategy) {
>     a <- df_a[[strategy]]
>     b <- df_b[[strategy]]
>     t_result <- t.test(a, b)
>     tibble(
>       strategy = strategy,
>       prop_classic = mean(a, na.rm = TRUE),
>       prop_other = mean(b, na.rm = TRUE),
>       diff = mean(b, na.rm = TRUE) - mean(a, na.rm = TRUE),
>       ci_lower = t_result$conf.int[1],
>       ci_upper = t_result$conf.int[2],
>       other_label = name_b
>     )
>   })
> }
> results_convo_unfolding <- convo_results(classic_means, full_means, "Unfolding")
> results_convo_kirk      <- convo_results(classic_means, kirk_means, "Kirk")
> plot_data_convo_unfolding <- results_convo_unfolding %>%
>   label_strategy() %>%
>   mutate(ci_diff_lower = -ci_upper, ci_diff_upper = -ci_lower)
> plot_data_convo_kirk <- results_convo_kirk %>%
>   label_strategy() %>%
>   mutate(ci_diff_lower = -ci_upper, ci_diff_upper = -ci_lower)
> p_unfolding_convo <- ggplot(plot_data_convo_unfolding %>% filter(strategy != "none_of_these"),
>                             aes(x = fct_reorder(strategy_clean, diff), y = diff, fill = strategy_clean)) +

>   coord_flip() +

> plot_data_convo_grouped <- map_df(strategy_vars, function(strategy) {
>   classic_vals <- classic_means[[strategy]]
>   trump_vals <- full_means[[strategy]]
>   kirk_vals <- kirk_means[[strategy]]
> 
>   classic_p <- mean(classic_vals, na.rm = TRUE)
>   trump_p <- mean(trump_vals, na.rm = TRUE)
>   kirk_p <- mean(kirk_vals, na.rm = TRUE)
> 
>   classic_n <- sum(!is.na(classic_vals))
>   trump_n <- sum(!is.na(trump_vals))
>   kirk_n <- sum(!is.na(kirk_vals))
> 
>   classic_se <- sqrt(classic_p * (1 - classic_p) / classic_n)
>   trump_se <- sqrt(trump_p * (1 - trump_p) / trump_n)
>   kirk_se <- sqrt(kirk_p * (1 - kirk_p) / kirk_n)
> 
>   tibble(
>     strategy = strategy,
>     strategy_clean = label_strategy(tibble(strategy = strategy))$strategy_clean,
>     Classic = classic_p,
>     `Trump (Unfolding)` = trump_p,
>     Kirk = kirk_p,
>     Classic_se = classic_se,
>     `Trump (Unfolding)_se` = trump_se,
>     Kirk_se = kirk_se
>   )
> }) %>%
>   filter(strategy != "none_of_these") %>%
>   pivot_longer(
>     cols = c(Classic, `Trump (Unfolding)`, Kirk),
>     names_to = "Condition",
>     values_to = "Proportion"
>   ) %>%
>   mutate(
>     se = case_when(
>       Condition == "Classic" ~ Classic_se,
>       Condition == "Trump (Unfolding)" ~ `Trump (Unfolding)_se`,
>       Condition == "Kirk" ~ Kirk_se
>     ),
>     ci_lower = pmax(0, Proportion - 1.96 * se),
>     ci_upper = pmin(1, Proportion + 1.96 * se),
>     strategy_clean = factor(strategy_clean, levels = strategy_order),
>     Condition = factor(Condition, levels = c("Classic", "Trump (Unfolding)", "Kirk"))
>   )
> ggplot(
>   plot_data_convo_grouped,
>   aes(x = strategy_clean, y = Proportion, fill = Condition)

>   ) +

>   ) +
>   labs(

>   theme_minimal(base_size = 18) +

==== 08_mediation ====
> RES <- load_results()
> CO <- load_cohorts()
> NBOOT <- 5000
> fit_b <- function(y, X) .lm.fit(cbind(1, X), y)$coefficients
> pct   <- function(v) unname(quantile(v, c(0.025, 0.975), type = 7))
> mediate <- function(an, oc) {
>   cc <- an %>% filter(!is.na(.data[[oc]]) & !is.na(ck0) & !is.na(ck1)) %>% mutate(y = .data[[oc]])
>   m_a <- lmr(ck1 ~ tx + ck0, cc)
>   m_b <- lmr(y ~ tx + ck1 + ck0, cc)
>   m_c <- lmr(y ~ tx + ck0, cc)
>   a <- term_lmr(m_a, "tx"); b <- term_lmr(m_b, "ck1")
>   dir <- term_lmr(m_b, "tx"); tot <- term_lmr(m_c, "tx")
>   n <- nrow(cc); y <- cc$y; t <- cc$tx; m1 <- cc$ck1; m0 <- cc$ck0
>   set.seed(SEED)
>   ind <- dire <- totb <- numeric(NBOOT)
>   for (k in seq_len(NBOOT)) {
>     i  <- sample.int(n, n, replace = TRUE)
>     ba <- fit_b(m1[i], cbind(t[i], m0[i]))[2]
>     bb <- fit_b(y[i], cbind(t[i], m1[i], m0[i]))
>     ind[k] <- ba * bb[3]; dire[k] <- bb[2]; totb[k] <- ba * bb[3] + bb[2]
>   }
>   pm <- ind / totb; pm <- pm[is.finite(pm)]
>   list(n = n, a = a, b = b,
>        direct = c(dir, list(boot_ci = pct(dire))),
>        total  = c(tot, list(boot_ci = pct(totb))),
>        indirect = list(b = a$b * b$b, boot_ci = pct(ind),
>                        boot_p = 2 * min(mean(ind >= 0), mean(ind <= 0))),
>        prop_mediated = list(est = if (abs(tot$b) > 1e-9) a$b * b$b / tot$b else NULL,
>                             boot_ci = if (length(pm) > 100) pct(pm) else NULL,
>                             note = "unstable when the total effect is near zero"),
>        nboot = NBOOT, seed = SEED)
> }
> descriptives <- function(an) {
>   ch <- an %>% filter(!is.na(ck1) & !is.na(ck0)) %>% mutate(d1 = ck1 - ck0)
>   list(n = nrow(an), arms = arm_counts(an$cond),
>        immediate_change_tx = mean(ch$d1[ch$tx == 1]), immediate_change_ctl = mean(ch$d1[ch$tx == 0]),
>        lds_mean = mean(an$lds, na.rm = TRUE), lds_sd = sd(an$lds, na.rm = TRUE),
>        gen_mean = mean(an$gen, na.rm = TRUE), gen_sd = sd(an$gen, na.rm = TRUE),
>        ck0_mean = mean(an$ck0, na.rm = TRUE))
> }
> MED <- list()
> for (nm in c("itt", "pp")) {
>   ds <- if (nm == "itt") CO$K_ITT else CO$K_PP
>   an <- ds %>% filter(returned == 1 & cond %in% ARMS) %>% mutate(tx = as.numeric(cond == "Tx"))
>   MED[[nm]] <- list(descriptives = descriptives(an))
>   for (oc in c("gen", "lds")) MED[[nm]][[oc]] <- mediate(an, oc)
> }
> RES$mediation <- MED
> save_results(RES)
> lab <- c(itt = sprintf("ITT (%d)", MED$itt$descriptives$n), pp = sprintf("PP (%d)", MED$pp$descriptives$n))
> med_tab <- bind_rows(lapply(c("itt", "pp"), function(nm) bind_rows(lapply(c("lds", "gen"), function(oc) {

>          b = r$b$b, b_lo = r$b$lo, b_hi = r$b$hi, b_p = r$b$p,
>          indirect = r$indirect$b, indirect_boot_lo = r$indirect$boot_ci[1],
>          indirect_boot_hi = r$indirect$boot_ci[2], indirect_boot_p = r$indirect$boot_p,
>          direct = r$direct$b, direct_lo = r$direct$lo, direct_hi = r$direct$hi, direct_p = r$direct$p,
>          direct_boot_lo = r$direct$boot_ci[1], direct_boot_hi = r$direct$boot_ci[2],
>          total = r$total$b, total_lo = r$total$lo, total_hi = r$total$hi, total_p = r$total$p,
>          total_boot_lo = r$total$boot_ci[1], total_boot_hi = r$total$boot_ci[2],
>          prop_mediated = if (is.null(r$prop_mediated$est)) NA_real_ else r$prop_mediated$est,
>          nboot = r$nboot, seed = r$seed)
> }))))
> write_table(med_tab, "mediation.csv")
