> GLM_CTRL <- glm.control(epsilon = 1e-12, maxit = 100)
> fit_return <- function(Z, r) {
>   X <- cbind(intercept = 1, Z)
>   f <- suppressWarnings(glm.fit(X, r, family = binomial(), control = GLM_CTRL))
>   p <- f$fitted.values
>   ok <- isTRUE(f$converged) && !isTRUE(f$boundary) && f$rank == ncol(X) && !anyNA(f$coefficients) &&
>     all(is.finite(p)) && min(p) > 1e-10 && max(p) < 1 - 1e-10
>   list(ok = ok, converged = isTRUE(f$converged), coef = f$coefficients, p = p, iter = f$iter)
> }
> ipw_weights <- function(D, covs) {
>   p <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(D)); fits <- list(); ok <- TRUE
>   for (arm in c("tx", "ctl")) {
>     rows <- which(D$DD == as.numeric(arm == "tx"))
>     f <- fit_return(as.matrix(D[rows, covs, drop = FALSE]), D$returned[rows])
>     fits[[arm]] <- f; ok <- ok && f$ok; p[rows] <- f$p
>   }
>   list(ok = ok, p = p, w = ifelse(D$returned == 1, 1 / p, NA_real_), fits = fits)
> }
> w_summary <- function(w) list(n_returned = length(w), min = min(w), max = max(w), mean = mean(w),
>                               p99 = unname(quantile(w, 0.99, type = 7)), sum = sum(w),
>                               ess = sum(w)^2 / sum(w^2))
> return_se <- function(Z, p) {
>   X <- cbind(intercept = 1, Z)
>   se <- sqrt(diag(solve(crossprod(X * (p * (1 - p)), X))))
>   setNames(se, colnames(X))
> }
> ipw_diagnostics <- function(D, ww, covs) {
>   sel <- list(tx = D$DD == 1, ctl = D$DD == 0, all = rep(TRUE, nrow(D)))
>   rm <- lapply(setNames(names(sel), names(sel)), function(a) {
>     s <- sel[[a]]; ret <- s & D$returned == 1
>     base <- list(n = sum(s), n_returned = sum(ret))
>     if (a != "all") base <- c(base, list(converged = ww$fits[[a]]$converged, iterations = ww$fits[[a]]$iter,
>                                          coef = as.list(ww$fits[[a]]$coef),
>                                          se = as.list(return_se(as.matrix(D[s, covs, drop = FALSE]), ww$p[s]))))
>     c(base, list(p_hat_min = min(ww$p[s]), p_hat_max = max(ww$p[s]),
>                  p_hat_min_returnees = min(ww$p[ret]), p_hat_max_returnees = max(ww$p[ret]),
>                  auc = auc_fn(ww$p[s], D$returned[s])))
>   })
>   # weights among returnees, plus n randomized, the fitted-probability range and the AUC of the same group
>   # (same fields, under the same names, as the Python implementation's "weights" block)
>   wt <- lapply(setNames(names(sel), names(sel)), function(a) {
>     s <- sel[[a]]
>     c(list(n = sum(s)), w_summary(ww$w[s & D$returned == 1]),
>       rm[[a]][c("p_hat_min", "p_hat_max", "p_hat_min_returnees", "p_hat_max_returnees", "auc")])
>   })
>   bal <- lapply(sel, function(s) {
>     ret <- s & D$returned == 1
>     lapply(setNames(covs, covs), function(v) {
>       x <- D[[v]]; mf <- mean(x[s]); sf <- sd(x[s])           # SD: n - 1 denominator
>       mu <- mean(x[ret]); mw <- sum(ww$w[ret] * x[ret]) / sum(ww$w[ret])
>       list(mean_all = mf, sd_all = sf, mean_returned = mu, mean_returned_weighted = mw,
>            smd_unweighted = (mu - mf) / sf, smd_weighted = (mw - mf) / sf)
>     })
>   })
>   list(return_model = rm, weights = wt, balance = bal)
> }
> sens_weights_block <- function(D, ww, covs, with_model = TRUE) {
>   dg <- ipw_diagnostics(D, ww, covs)
>   c(if (with_model) list(return_model = dg$return_model[c("tx", "ctl")]), dg$weights)
> }
> CHECK_MAX <- c(wls_vs_lm_robust = 0, wlogit_vs_glm = 0, wlogit_vs_sandwich = 0)
> wls_fit <- function(y, X, w, inference = TRUE, check = FALSE) {
>   sw <- sqrt(w); Xw <- X * sw; yw <- y * sw
>   q <- qr(Xw)
>   if (q$rank < ncol(X)) stop("singular design")
>   b <- qr.coef(q, yw); names(b) <- colnames(X)
>   n <- length(y); k <- ncol(X)
>   if (!inference) return(list(coef = b, n = n))
>   ew   <- yw - drop(Xw %*% b)                    # whitened residuals
>   h    <- rowSums(qr.Q(q)^2)                     # leverage from the whitened design
>   XtXi <- chol2inv(qr.R(q))
>   V    <- XtXi %*% crossprod(Xw * (ew / sqrt(1 - h))) %*% XtXi
>   se   <- sqrt(diag(V)); names(se) <- colnames(X)
>   df   <- n - k; tcrit <- qt(0.975, df)
>   out  <- list(coef = b, se = se, lo = b - tcrit * se, hi = b + tcrit * se,
>                p = 2 * pt(abs(b / se), df, lower.tail = FALSE), n = n, df = df)
>   if (check) {                                   # same model through estimatr::lm_robust
>     dd <- as.data.frame(X[, -1, drop = FALSE]); dd$.y <- y; dd$.w <- w
>     m  <- lm_robust(.y ~ . - .w, data = dd, weights = .w, se_type = "HC2")
>     gap <- max(abs(unname(m$coefficients) - unname(b)), abs(unname(m$std.error) - unname(se)),
>                abs(unname(m$conf.low) - unname(out$lo)), abs(unname(m$conf.high) - unname(out$hi)),
>                abs(unname(m$p.value) - unname(out$p)))
>     CHECK_MAX["wls_vs_lm_robust"] <<- max(CHECK_MAX["wls_vs_lm_robust"], gap)
>     if (gap > 1e-7) stop("hand-coded weighted HC2 and lm_robust(weights, HC2) disagree: ", gap)
>   }
>   out
> }
> term_w <- function(f, name) {
>   if (is.null(f$se)) return(list(b = unname(f$coef[name]), n = f$n))
>   list(b = unname(f$coef[name]), se = unname(f$se[name]), lo = unname(f$lo[name]), hi = unname(f$hi[name]),
>        p = unname(f$p[name]), n = f$n)
> }
> wlogit_fit <- function(y, X, w, inference = TRUE, check = FALSE, maxit = 100, tol = 1e-10) {
>   k <- ncol(X); beta <- rep(0, k); conv <- FALSE
>   for (it in seq_len(maxit)) {
>     mu   <- plogis(drop(X %*% beta))
>     A    <- crossprod(X * (w * mu * (1 - mu)), X)
>     step <- tryCatch(drop(solve(A, crossprod(X, w * (y - mu)))), error = function(e) NULL)
>     if (is.null(step) || any(!is.finite(step))) stop("singular design")
>     beta <- beta + step
>     if (max(abs(step)) < tol) { conv <- TRUE; break }
>   }
>   if (!conv || max(abs(beta)) > 30) stop("logistic model did not converge")
>   names(beta) <- colnames(X); n <- length(y)
>   if (!inference) return(list(coef = beta, n = n))
>   mu <- plogis(drop(X %*% beta))
>   Ai <- solve(crossprod(X * (w * mu * (1 - mu)), X))        # A = sum w mu (1 - mu) x x'
>   B  <- crossprod(X * (w * (y - mu)))                       # B = sum w^2 (y - mu)^2 x x'
>   V  <- Ai %*% B %*% Ai
>   se <- sqrt(diag(V)); names(se) <- colnames(X)
>   if (check) {
>     dd <- as.data.frame(X[, -1, drop = FALSE]); dd$.y <- y; dd$.w <- w
>     m  <- suppressWarnings(glm(.y ~ . - .w, data = dd, weights = .w, family = binomial,
>                                control = glm.control(epsilon = 1e-12, maxit = 100)))
>     gap <- max(abs(unname(coef(m)) - unname(beta)))
>     CHECK_MAX["wlogit_vs_glm"] <<- max(CHECK_MAX["wlogit_vs_glm"], gap)
>     if (gap > 1e-6) stop("hand-coded weighted logit and glm(weights) disagree: ", gap)
>     if (requireNamespace("sandwich", quietly = TRUE)) {
>       gap2 <- max(abs(sqrt(diag(sandwich::vcovHC(m, type = "HC0"))) - se))
>       CHECK_MAX["wlogit_vs_sandwich"] <<- max(CHECK_MAX["wlogit_vs_sandwich"], gap2)
>       if (gap2 > 1e-6) stop("hand-coded HC0 sandwich and sandwich::vcovHC disagree: ", gap2)
>     }
>   }
>   list(coef = beta, se = se, n = n)
> }
> term_logit <- function(f, name) {
>   b <- unname(f$coef[name])
>   if (is.null(f$se)) return(list(b = b, n = f$n))
>   se <- unname(f$se[name])
>   list(b = b, se = se, or = exp(b), lo = exp(b - Z975 * se), hi = exp(b + Z975 * se),
>        p = 2 * pnorm(abs(b / se), lower.tail = FALSE), n = f$n)
> }
> kirk_models <- function(R, w, inference = TRUE, check = FALSE) {
>   fit <- function(y, X, rows) wls_fit(y[rows], X[rows, , drop = FALSE], w[rows], inference, check)
>   out <- list()
>   for (oc in c("lds", "gen")) {
>     y  <- R[[oc]]
>     r1 <- !is.na(y) & !is.na(R$pre_cust)
>     out[[paste0("anc_", oc, "_precust")]] <- term_w(fit(y, cbind(const = 1, DD = R$DD, pre_cust = R$pre_cust), r1), "DD")
>     r2 <- !is.na(y) & !is.na(R$ck0)
>     X_tot <- cbind(const = 1, DD = R$DD, ck0 = R$ck0)
>     out[[paste0("anc_", oc)]] <- term_w(fit(y, X_tot, r2), "DD")
>     r3 <- r2 & !is.na(R$ck1)
>     out[[paste0("lin_", oc)]] <- term_w(fit(y - R$ck0, cbind(const = 1, d1 = R$ck1 - R$ck0, ck0 = R$ck0), r3), "d1")
>     fa <- fit(R$ck1, X_tot, r3)
>     fb <- fit(y, cbind(const = 1, DD = R$DD, ck1 = R$ck1, ck0 = R$ck0), r3)
>     fc <- fit(y, X_tot, r3)
>     a <- term_w(fa, "DD"); b <- term_w(fb, "ck1")
>     out[[paste0("med_", oc)]] <- list(n = sum(r3), a = a, b = b,
>                                       direct = term_w(fb, "DD"), total = term_w(fc, "DD"),
>                                       indirect = list(b = a$b * b$b))
>   }
>   out[c("anc_lds_precust", "anc_gen_precust", "anc_lds", "anc_gen", "lin_lds", "lin_gen", "med_gen", "med_lds")]
> }
> K_SIMPLE <- c("anc_lds_precust", "anc_gen_precust", "anc_lds", "anc_gen", "lin_lds", "lin_gen")
> K_MED    <- c("med_gen", "med_lds")
> MED_PARTS <- c("a", "b", "direct", "total", "indirect")
> kirk_point <- function(o) {
>   v <- sapply(K_SIMPLE, function(k) o[[k]]$b)
>   for (m in K_MED) v <- c(v, setNames(sapply(MED_PARTS, function(p) o[[m]][[p]]$b), paste0(m, ".", MED_PARTS)))
>   v
> }
> kirk_attach_boot <- function(o, bt) {
>   ci <- apply(bt$est, 2, pct); s <- apply(bt$est, 2, sd, na.rm = TRUE)
>   for (k in K_SIMPLE) o[[k]] <- c(o[[k]], list(boot_lo = ci[1, k], boot_hi = ci[2, k], boot_se = s[[k]]))
>   for (m in K_MED) for (p in MED_PARTS) {
>     nm <- paste0(m, ".", p)
>     o[[m]][[p]] <- c(o[[m]][[p]], list(boot_lo = ci[1, nm], boot_hi = ci[2, nm], boot_se = s[[nm]]))
>   }
>   o$boot_failed <- bt$failed
>   o
> }
> T_OUTS <- c("whoknows", "whoknows_alt", "hidden_bin")
> trump_models <- function(R, w, inference = TRUE, check = FALSE) {
>   out <- list()
>   for (oc in T_OUTS) {
>     y <- R[[oc]]; r <- !is.na(y) & !is.na(R$pc)
>     out[[oc]] <- term_logit(wlogit_fit(y[r], cbind(const = 1, DD = R$DD[r], pc = R$pc[r]), w[r], inference, check), "DD")
>   }
>   out
> }
> trump_point <- function(o) sapply(T_OUTS, function(k) o[[k]]$b)
> trump_attach_boot <- function(o, bt) {
>   ci <- apply(bt$est, 2, pct); s <- apply(bt$est, 2, sd, na.rm = TRUE)
>   for (k in T_OUTS) o[[k]] <- c(o[[k]], list(boot_lo = exp(ci[1, k]), boot_hi = exp(ci[2, k]),
>                                               boot_b_lo = ci[1, k], boot_b_hi = ci[2, k],   # log-odds scale
>                                               boot_se = s[[k]]))                            # SD of the log-odds draws
>   o$boot_failed <- bt$failed
>   o
> }
> boot_ipw <- function(D, covs, model_fun, point_fun, nboot = NBOOT) {
>   ix1 <- which(D$DD == 1); ix0 <- which(D$DD == 0)
>   est <- NULL; failed <- 0L
>   for (b in seq_len(nboot)) {
>     idx <- c(ix1[sample.int(length(ix1), replace = TRUE)], ix0[sample.int(length(ix0), replace = TRUE)])
>     Db  <- D[idx, , drop = FALSE]
>     v <- tryCatch({
>       ww <- ipw_weights(Db, covs)
>       if (!ww$ok) stop("return model did not converge")
>       ret <- Db$returned == 1
>       pt  <- point_fun(model_fun(Db[ret, , drop = FALSE], ww$w[ret], inference = FALSE))
>       if (!all(is.finite(pt))) stop("non-finite estimate")
>       pt
>     }, error = function(e) NULL)
>     if (is.null(v)) { failed <- failed + 1L; next }
>     if (is.null(est)) est <- matrix(NA_real_, nboot, length(v), dimnames = list(NULL, names(v)))
>     est[b, ] <- v
>   }
>   list(est = est, failed = failed)
> }
> completion_estimable <- function(D) {             # can the completion indicator enter the return model?
>   msg <- character(0)
>   for (arm in c("tx", "ctl")) {
>     s <- D$DD == as.numeric(arm == "tx"); nc <- s & D$completed_post == 0
>     if (sum(nc) == 0 || sum(nc) == sum(s)) {
>       msg <- c(msg, sprintf("%s arm: the completion indicator is constant", arm))
>     } else if (sum(D$returned[nc]) == 0 || sum(D$returned[nc]) == sum(nc)) {
>       msg <- c(msg, sprintf("%s arm: %d of the %d participants who quit before the post-treatment measures returned",
>                             arm, sum(D$returned[nc]), sum(nc)))
>     }
>   }
>   list(estimable = length(msg) == 0, reason = paste(msg, collapse = "; "))
> }
> quit_table <- function(D) {                       # same fields as the Python implementation's quit_by_arm
>   lapply(c(tx = 1, ctl = 0), function(a) {
>     s <- D$DD == a; q <- s & D$completed_post == 0; cpl <- s & D$completed_post == 1
>     list(n_quit = sum(q), n_quit_returned = sum(D$returned[q]), n_completed = sum(cpl), n_completed_returned = sum(D$returned[cpl]))
>   })
> }
> run_study <- function(D, model_fun, point_fun, attach_fun, label) {
>   ret <- D$returned == 1; R <- D[ret, , drop = FALSE]
>   ww  <- ipw_weights(D, COVS)
>   if (!ww$ok) stop(label, ": primary return model failed")
>   diag <- ipw_diagnostics(D, ww, COVS)
>   w    <- ww$w[ret]
>   unw  <- model_fun(R, rep(1, nrow(R)), inference = TRUE, check = TRUE)
>   ipw  <- model_fun(R, w, inference = TRUE, check = TRUE)
>   cat(label, ": bootstrap (", NBOOT, " resamples) ...\n", sep = "")
>   bt   <- boot_ipw(D, COVS, model_fun, point_fun)
>   ipw  <- attach_fun(ipw, bt)
>   # E. sensitivity
>   # (models under sens$<specification>; return model and weight summaries under sens_weights$<specification>)
>   cap  <- unname(quantile(w, 0.99, type = 7))
>   w_tr <- pmin(w, cap)
>   s_tr <- model_fun(R, w_tr, inference = TRUE, check = TRUE)
>   ww_tr <- ww; ww_tr$w <- pmin(ww$w, cap)          # same return model; the returnees' weights capped
>   sw <- list(trunc99 = c(list(cap = cap, n_truncated = sum(w > cap)),
>                          sens_weights_block(D, ww_tr, COVS, with_model = FALSE)))
>   wp   <- ipw_weights(D, COVS_PARS)
>   if (!wp$ok) stop(label, ": parsimonious return model failed")
>   s_pa <- model_fun(R, wp$w[ret], inference = TRUE, check = TRUE)
>   sw$parsimonious <- sens_weights_block(D, wp, COVS_PARS)
>   ce <- completion_estimable(D)
>   if (ce$estimable) {
>     covs_c <- c(COVS, "completed_post")
>     wc <- ipw_weights(D, covs_c)
>     if (!wc$ok) stop(label, ": completion return model failed")
>     s_co <- c(model_fun(R, wc$w[ret], inference = TRUE, check = TRUE),
>               list(estimable = TRUE, quit_by_arm = quit_table(D)))
>     swc <- sens_weights_block(D, wc, covs_c)
>     sw$completion <- c(swc["return_model"], list(quit_by_arm = quit_table(D)), swc[c("tx", "ctl", "all")])
>   } else {
>     s_co <- list(estimable = FALSE, quit_by_arm = quit_table(D),
>                  reason = paste0("the completion indicator predicts non-return perfectly (", ce$reason,
>                                  "), so the return model with this indicator has no finite maximum-likelihood estimate"))
>   }
>   list(n_randomized = nrow(D), n_returned = sum(ret),
>        return_model = diag$return_model, weights = diag$weights, balance = diag$balance,
>        unweighted = unw, ipw = ipw,
>        sens = list(trunc99 = s_tr, parsimonious = s_pa, completion = s_co),
>        sens_weights = sw,
>        returned_by_cond = as.list(setNames(as.integer(table(factor(D$cond[ret], levels = ARMS))), ARMS)))
> }

> lee_core <- function(is_tx, y) {
>   obs_t <- y[is_tx & !is.na(y)]; obs_c <- y[!is_tx & !is.na(y)]
>   n_t <- sum(is_tx); n_c <- sum(!is_tx)
>   p_t <- length(obs_t) / n_t; p_c <- length(obs_c) / n_c
>   if (p_t >= p_c) {
>     tp <- 1 - p_c / p_t; s <- sort(obs_t); n <- length(s); k <- as.integer(round(n * tp))
>     b1 <- mean(s[(k + 1):n]) - mean(obs_c)        # lowest k removed
>     b2 <- mean(s[1:(n - k)]) - mean(obs_c)        # highest k removed
>   } else {
>     tp <- 1 - p_t / p_c; s <- sort(obs_c); n <- length(s); k <- as.integer(round(n * tp))
>     b1 <- mean(obs_t) - mean(s[1:(n - k)])
>     b2 <- mean(obs_t) - mean(s[(k + 1):n])
>   }
>   list(lo = min(b1, b2), hi = max(b1, b2), naive = mean(obs_t) - mean(obs_c),
>        p_t = p_t, p_c = p_c, tp = tp, k = k, n_t = n_t, n_c = n_c, tx_trimmed = p_t >= p_c)
> }
> lee_adjust <- function(is_tx, y, x) {
>   r <- !is.na(y)
>   beta <- qr.coef(qr(cbind(1, as.numeric(is_tx[r]), x[r])), y[r])[3]
>   y[r] <- y[r] - beta * (x[r] - mean(x[r]))
>   list(y = y, beta = unname(beta), xbar = mean(x[r]))
> }
> lee_entry <- function(is_tx, y, ctl_label, x = NULL, nboot = NBOOT) {
>   adj <- if (is.null(x)) NULL else lee_adjust(is_tx, y, x)
>   b <- lee_core(is_tx, if (is.null(x)) y else adj$y)
>   n <- length(y); bl <- bu <- rep(NA_real_, nboot)
>   for (i in seq_len(nboot)) {
>     idx <- sample.int(n, n, replace = TRUE)       # whole two-group sample, not stratified
>     r <- tryCatch(lee_core(is_tx[idx], if (is.null(x)) y[idx] else lee_adjust(is_tx[idx], y[idx], x[idx])$y),
>                   error = function(e) NULL)
>     if (!is.null(r) && is.finite(r$lo) && is.finite(r$hi)) { bl[i] <- r$lo; bu[i] <- r$hi }
>   }
>   out <- list(lo = b$lo, hi = b$hi, naive = b$naive, rate_tx = b$p_t, rate_ctl = b$p_c, trim = b$tp,
>               trimmed_arm = if (b$tx_trimmed) "Tx" else ctl_label, k = b$k, n_tx = b$n_t, n_ctl = b$n_c,
>               ci_lo = b$lo - 1.96 * sd0(bl), ci_hi = b$hi + 1.96 * sd0(bu),
>               boot_sd_lo = sd0(bl), boot_sd_hi = sd0(bu), boot_failed = sum(is.na(bl)))
>   if (!is.null(x)) out <- c(out, list(beta_pre_cust = adj$beta, mean_pre_cust_respondents = adj$xbar))
>   out
> }

> flatten <- function(x, prefix = "", flags = FALSE) {

>       out <- c(out, flatten(x[[i]], key, flags))

>   } else if (is.numeric(x) && length(x) == 1) {
>     out[[prefix]] <- x
>   } else if (flags && is.logical(x) && length(x) == 1 && !is.na(x)) {
>     out[[prefix]] <- as.numeric(x)

> tol_for <- function(key) {
>   leaf <- sub(".*\\.", "", key); parent <- sub("\\.[^.]*$", "", key)
>   # (kirk_dropouts_itt.<arm> are counts like kirk_dropouts.<arm>; imm3_*.lo_tukey / hi_tukey / d
>   #  take the coefficient rule; trump_dropout_chi2.df / N / arms.<arm> / dropouts.<arm> are counts)
>   if (leaf %in% COUNT_KEYS || grepl("\\.(pp_arms|itt_arms|arms|dropouts|flagged_by_belief|no_by_arm)\\.", key) ||
>       grepl("^kirk_dropouts(_itt)?\\.", key)) return(c(0, "count (exact)"))
>   if (leaf == "p" || leaf == "p_tukey" || leaf == "p3") return(c(0.002, "p (0.002)"))
>   if (grepl("^lee\\.", key) && leaf %in% c("ci_lo", "ci_hi")) return(c(0.3, "bootstrap CI (0.3)"))
>   if (grepl("^mediation\\.", key) && grepl("\\.indirect\\.boot_ci\\.[12]$", key))
>     return(c(0.1, "mediation bootstrap CI, indirect (0.1)"))
>   if (grepl("^mediation\\.", key) && grepl("\\.boot_ci\\.[12]$", key))
>     return(c(0.2, "mediation bootstrap CI, direct/total (0.2)"))
>   if (grepl("^mediation\\.", key) && leaf == "boot_p") return(c(0.01, "mediation bootstrap p (0.01)"))
>   c(0.01, "coefficient (0.01)")
> }

> n_skip_iterations <- sum(rep_ipw_all$rule == "iteration counter (not compared)")
> rep <- bind_rows(rep_res, rep_ipw)
> write_table(bind_rows(rep_res, rep_ipw_all), "validation_report.csv")
> fmt <- function(x) ifelse(abs(x) >= 1000, sprintf("%.1f", x), sprintf("%.5f", x))
> cat(sprintf("%-52s %14s %14s %10s %8s  %s\n", "quantity", "python", "R", "|diff|", "tol", "status"))
quantity                                                     python              R     |diff|      tol  status
> for (i in seq_len(nrow(rep))) {
>   cat(sprintf("%-52s %14s %14s %10.6f %8g  %s\n", substr(rep$key[i], 1, 52), fmt(rep$python[i]), fmt(rep$R[i]),
>               rep$abs_diff[i], rep$tolerance[i], rep$status[i]))
> }

> check_conspiracy_theory <- function(Conspiracies) {
>   completionObj<-create_chat_completion(
>     model = 'gpt-4o', 
>     max_tokens = 5,
>     temperature = 0,
>     messages = 
>       list(
>         list(role = 'system', content = 'Determine if the following question-responses (from a participant in an online academic survey) collectively contain or reflect AFFIRMATIVE belief in a conspiracy theory (or something quite like a conspiracy theory) 
>              concerning an event that occurred on July 13, 2024: the attempted assassination of Donald Trump. Notably, these question-responses were written in the week following the assanation attempt, when many conspiracy-like theories were swirling. For 
>              context, here is what was known at the time of the survey. <On July 13, 2024, former President Donald Trump survived an assassination attempt during a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. The shooter, identified as 20-year-old Thomas Matthew 
>              Crooks, opened fire from a rooftop approximately 410 feet away from the stage where Trump was speaking. Trump narrowly escaped fatal injury when a bullet grazed his right ear. He later described the experience as "surreal" and "miraculous". One 
>              bystander, 50-year-old firefighter Corey Comperatore, was killed in the attack. Two others were seriously wounded. Secret Service counter snipers neutralized Crooks within about 15 seconds of the initial shots. The assassination attempt is being 
>              investigated as a potential act of domestic terrorism. Crooks had no prior criminal history or military background.He was described as an intelligent loner with few friends and a limited social media presence. Crooks political affiliations remain 
>              unclear. He was registered as a Republican but had made a small donation to a progressive PAC. Investigators found a remote transmitter on Crooks that may have been intended to detonate suspicious devices found in his car and home. The FBI has 
>              accessed Crooks phone but has not yet uncovered significant information about his motives. The assassination attempt has intensified concerns about the deep political divide in the United States. Both Republicans and Democrats have attempted to 
>              attribute blame for the incident to their political opponents, despite a lack of clear evidence. President Biden urged Americans to "cool it down" in the wake of the attack. The incident has sparked debates about security measures at political 
>              events and the role of rhetoric in inciting violence. Trump has expressed a desire to use the incident as a catalyst for national unity, stating his intention to set aside divisive rhetoric and focus on bringing the country together.> We are asking 
>              you to complete this classification task because we are social science researchers who are testing the efficacy of an intervention that seeks to reduce recently-formed conspiratorial beliefs (i.e., such as those forming in the wake of the assassination attempt). 
>              To check whether participants are good candidates for the intervention, after they entered our experiment and we had them articulate, in their own words, whether or not they believed in a conspiracy concerning the assasination attempt. Particularly, 
>              they were asked the following two questions: <Q1: In the wake of the reported assassination attempt against former President Trump, numerous explanations have emerged, ranging from official accounts to alternative theories. Some people believe there 
>              may be more to the reported assassination attempt against former President Trump than what has been officially stated. To what extent do you think there might be hidden or unrevealed aspects to this event? Please explain your thoughts, including any 
>              alternative explanations you find plausible or any reasons you might doubt the official account.> <Q2: As applicable, could you share specific pieces of evidence, events, sources of information, or personal experiences that have particularly influenced 
>              your perspective? Please describe these in as much detail as you feel comfortable.> Your task is to evaluate these responses to determine whether the respondent is a good candidate testing the efficacy of our intervention (which is intended to reduce 
>              conspiracy beliefs concerning the assassination attempt). A good candidate will have at least some suspicion that a conspiracy (or something quite like a conspiracy)is behind the assassination attempt but could, of course, also be someone who already 
>              believes in a conspiracy. Other than anything else, we want to avoid including people who express little openness to the possibility of a conspiracy. If the participant is someone who has expressed enough conspiracy belief to make them a good candidate, 
>              respond only YES. If the response indicates that the respondent does not harbor any suspicions about a conspiracy concerning the event, respond only with NO. In cases where the answer is ambiguous, response only MAYBE. >'),
>         list(role = 'user', content = Conspiracies)
>       )
>   )
>   response <- completionObj$choices$message.content
>   return(response)
> }

> calculate_dppc2 <- function(data, pre_col, post_col, group_col) {
>   # Summarize data by group
>   summary_stats <- data %>%
>     group_by({{ group_col }}) %>%
>     summarise(
>       pre_mean = mean({{ pre_col }}, na.rm = TRUE),
>       pre_sd = sd({{ pre_col }}, na.rm = TRUE),
>       post_mean = mean({{ post_col }}, na.rm = TRUE),
>       post_sd = sd({{ post_col }}, na.rm = TRUE),
>       n = n(),
>       .groups = 'drop'
>     )
>   
>   # Extract treatment and control stats
>   T.n <- summary_stats[2, ]$n
>   C.n <- summary_stats[1, ]$n
>   
>   T.sd_pre <- summary_stats[2, ]$pre_sd
>   C.sd_pre <- summary_stats[1, ]$pre_sd
>   
>   T.m_post <- summary_stats[2, ]$post_mean
>   C.m_post <- summary_stats[1, ]$post_mean
>   
>   T.m_pre <- summary_stats[2, ]$pre_mean
>   C.m_pre <- summary_stats[1, ]$pre_mean
>   
>   # Calculate pooled standard deviation
>   sd.pooled <- sqrt(((T.n - 1) * T.sd_pre^2 + (C.n - 1) * C.sd_pre^2) / (T.n + C.n - 2))
>   
>   # Calculate the effect size using Cohen's method
>   yi <- metafor:::.cmicalc(T.n + C.n - 2) * ((T.m_post - T.m_pre) - (C.m_post - C.m_pre)) / sd.pooled
>   
>   # Return a list containing all computed values
>   list(
>     treatment_n = T.n,
>     control_n = C.n,
>     treatment_pre_sd = round(T.sd_pre, 2),
>     control_pre_sd = round(C.sd_pre, 2),
>     treatment_post_mean = round(T.m_post, 2),
>     control_post_mean = round(C.m_post, 2),
>     treatment_pre_mean = round(T.m_pre, 2),
>     control_pre_mean = round(C.m_pre, 2),
>     pooled_sd = round(sd.pooled, 2),
>     effect_size = round(yi, 2)
>   )
> }

Duplicate files across repo mirrors

1 file is byte-identical to another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component that mirrors the same materials). It was only run once, from its first occurrence, to avoid wasted duplicate execution: VOR_05_unfolding_conspiracies_main_analysis_exp_2.qmd at OSF_package_2026-10-19.zip/OSF_package_2026-10-19/2_original_analyses/experiment_2_Kirk/VOR_05_unfolding_conspiracies_main_analysis_exp_2.qmd (same as VOR_05_unfolding_conspiracies_main_analysis_exp_2.qmd at OSF_package_2026-10-19.zip/OSF_package_2026-10-19/1_revision_pipeline/data/experiment_2_Kirk/VOR_05_unfolding_conspiracies_main_analysis_exp_2.qmd).

Python code

This module also assesses whether the paper’s Python code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 5 Python code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first) and numeric filename prefixes. Python has no source()-equivalent import-based ordering signal (an import loads a module, not the paper’s own analysis flow), so that basis never applies here.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 r2_battery.py — numeric
2 r2_mediation.py r2_battery.py dependency
3 r2_ipw.py r2_battery.py, r2_mediation.py dependency
4 deidentify.py — none
5 make_si_tables.py — none

File paths

1 data path in the code does not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed it to where the file is, so the code could run: analysis/r2_ipw.json and analysis/r2_mediation.json to analysis/r2_mediation.json (in make_si_tables.py). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find the file. The code reads files that are only inside OSF_package_2026-10-19.zip, and no script unpacks it. We unpacked it in its folder before the run. So that others can run the code as deposited, start the code with a line that unpacks it (such as zipfile.ZipFile("OSF_package_2026-10-19.zip").extractall() in Python), or upload the files unpacked.

Execution

The Python code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 5 scripts: 4 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a requirements.txt).

Messages / errors (stderr):


deidentify.py -- build the de-identified copies of the study's data files for both parts of the
deposit: ../../2_original_analyses (every data file of the authors' original OSF folder, beside the
original analysis scripts, reports and figures) and this folder (the data files that the code in
../code reads).

Usage
    python3 deidentify.py ORIGINAL_DATA_DIR [PACKAGE_DIR]

ORIGINAL_DATA_DIR is the authors' original data and analysis folder (subfolders experiment_1_Trump/,
experiment_2_Kirk/, experiment_1_and_2_argument_coding/, figures/).  Its files are only read.
PACKAGE_DIR (default: two folders above this script) is the folder that holds 1_revision_pipeline/
and 2_original_analyses/.  The script writes

  * 2_original_analyses/<same relative path>: a de-identified copy of every CSV file of
    ORIGINAL_DATA_DIR, and an unchanged copy of every other file (analysis scripts, rendered
    reports, figure PDFs), after checking them (see "Non-tabular files" below);
  * 1_revision_pipeline/data/<same relative path>: the de-identified copies of the ten CSV files in
    PIPELINE_FILES (identical to their copies in 2_original_analyses) and an unchanged copy of the
    archived Experiment 2 analysis script that ../code/pipeline/vor05_itt re-runs.

For every CSV file the script

  1. removes the columns IPAddress, LocationLatitude, LocationLongitude, RecipientEmail,
     RecipientFirstName, RecipientLastName, ExternalReference, assignmentid, projectid, rid,
     PROLIFIC_PID, SESSION_ID and STUDY_ID, and every column whose name starts with "BrowserInfo_"
     (names compared without regard to upper / lower case);

  2. edits the chat platform's logs, the JSON that the platform wrote into survey fields (Q2,
     ChatHistory ... ChatHistory6, chathistory1 ... chathistory6; see CHAT_LOGS).  It removes the
     browser and device information (every "userAgent" / "userAgentInfo" object: user-agent string,
     browser, operating system, device, screen size) and the chat platform's encrypted API key
     ("apiKeyEncrypted" in chatParams.model), and applies steps 4 and 5 to the text of every message.
     Messages, timestamps and every other entry are kept, and a log in which nothing changes is left
     as it is.  A log too long for one field continues in the next field(s), each field holding a
     JSON string with one piece of the log; such a log is joined, edited and cut again into pieces of
     the same kind (Experiment 1: six pieces of equal length; Experiment 2: pieces of at most 19,000
     characters), and fields left without a piece are left empty.  The edited JSON is written in the
     platform's own format (no spaces, non-ASCII characters unescaped); before editing, the script
     checks that this format reproduces every original log exactly;

  3. replaces every participantId by an anonymous code.  The distinct non-blank participantId values
     of the data rows of ALL CSV files of ORIGINAL_DATA_DIR (and the participant IDs that the
     Experiment 1 chat platform repeated inside its logs, all of which also occur in a participantId
     column) are pooled and sorted as strings; the k-th value becomes "P" followed by k, zero-padded
     to the width of the largest k (P0001, P0002, ...).  The same original value receives the same
     code in every file of both parts, so the main surveys, the follow-up surveys and the derived
     files can still be linked, and sorting by the code gives the same order as sorting by the
     original value.  Blank values (and "NA" in files written by R) stay as they are.  The extra
     header rows of Qualtrics exports (question text and import ids) are left as they are;

  4. replaces an original participantId that occurs inside any other text field by the same code;

  5. replaces e-mail addresses, telephone numbers, and any value of a removed identifier column (IP
     address, panel assignment / project / session / study id, coder panel id, recipient fields)
     that occurs inside another text field by "[redacted]".

Everything else is kept byte for byte: the order of the rows and of the remaining columns, the
Qualtrics header rows, the quoting of every field, the line endings (including line breaks inside
quoted fields), the UTF-8 encoding and the absence of a newline after the last record.  A field is
re-quoted only if its content changed, and then in the style of the original field.  The script
checks that its CSV reader returns exactly what Python's csv module returns, that re-assembling the
parsed file gives back the original bytes, that no original participantId, no value of a removed
identifier column and no encrypted API key is left in any output file, and that every edited chat
log is valid JSON without the removed entries.  A CSV file in which nothing changes is copied
unchanged.

Non-tabular files are copied unchanged after these checks: analysis scripts (.R, .qmd) must not
contain an API key (only placeholders such as Sys.setenv(OPENAI_API_KEY = '...') are allowed);
rendered reports (.html) are searched, outside their embedded base64 data (images, fonts, libraries),
for original participant IDs (replaced by their codes), IP addresses and other values of removed identifier
columns, e-mail addresses, user-agent strings and API keys (replaced by "[redacted]"); figure PDFs
(.pdf) are searched, after decompression, for the same values and are never edited (the script stops
if one is found).  macOS metadata files (.DS_Store) are skipped.

The mapping from original participantIds to codes exists only in memory while the script runs; it is
never printed or written to disk.  The script prints counts only.

76 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 44 matched (43 fully, 1 partially) — 57.9% found.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The “Plausible” column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output’s own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

Participants were then randomly assigned to (1) a Debunking Dialogue condition in which the LLM tried to reduce their conspiratorial belief, (2) an Informational List condition in which they were shown a static list of the facts currently available about the event, or (3) an Irrelevant Dialogue control in which they discussed a topic unrelated to the event with the LLM.

Participants in the study were US adults recruited through the CloudResearch platform.

Participants gave informed consent, completed several attention screens, provided basic demographics, and answered questions about their beliefs about AI.

Participants were then asked to “share specific pieces of evidence, events, sources of information, or personal experiences that have particularly influenced [their] perspective. . . in as much detail as [they] feel comfortable.”

Participants were then randomly assigned to the conspiracy beliefs dialogue treatment (50%), the static information treatment (25%), or the irrelevant dialogue control (25%).

Participants in the study were US adults recruited through the CloudResearch platform. 2249 people began the survey during the experiment period.

Participants gave informed consent, completed attention screens, provided basic demographics, and answered a question about trust in AI.

We recruited US adults on Prolific (native English speakers who were Prolific verified “Qualified AI”-category respondents, a premium tier of participants who have passed targeted skill assessments or demonstrated verified experience in tasks required for AI model training and evaluation, and were blind to researcher expectations) between January 22 and February 1, 2026, and had them code a subset of 300 randomly selected sentences from the AI turns.

To check whether participants are good candidates for the intervention, after they entered our experiment and we had them articulate, in their own words, whether or not they believed in a conspiracy concerning the assassination attempt.

To check whether participants are good candidates for the intervention, after they entered our experiment we had them articulate, in their own words, whether or not they believed in a conspiracy concerning the assasination attempt.

Three of the 37 participants had already been removed by the pre-randomization survey-agent screen (a hidden instruction designed to detect automated respondents).

The experiment was deemed exempt by MIT’s institutional review board.

As before, the experiment was built with Qualtrics and deemed exempt by the MIT IRB.
