LLM rhetorical strategies

Having demonstrated that the AI was indeed able to reduce conspiracy beliefs in the immediate aftermath of these crisis events, we now examine which persuasion strategies the AI used to do so. We developed a qualitative coding procedure that could be executed at scale by an LLM yet validated by human raters (see Methods for details).

The results are shown in Figure 2. For the Trump assassination attempt, where virtually no information was available about the would-be assassin and his motives, the pattern for strategy use by the AI was notably different from the strategies that the same coding procedure identifies in the dialogues about classic conspiracies from Costello et al. 4 To debunk the Trump assassination attempt conspiracies, the AI relied less on rational persuasion (9.7 percentage points less than in classic conspiracy conversations, χ 2 (1) = 487, p < .001) and more on the prudence of epistemic caution when little is known (7.2 points more, χ 2 (1) = 544, p < .001), asking open-ended questions designed to facilitate reflection (5.2 points more, χ 2 (1) = 1023, p < .001), and encouraging reliance on credible sources (6.2 points more, χ 2 (1) = 564, p < .001). Conversely, when debunking conspiracies related to the Kirk assassination-where more information about the assassin and his motives was known, albeit still less information than for most classic conspiracies-the AI employed similar strategies to those used for debunking classic conspiracies, though it placed somewhat greater emphasis on highlighting harms (7.4 percentage points more than in classic conspiracy conversations, χ 2 (1) = 2325, p < .001).

Effects on subsequent conspiratorial beliefs

Finally, we ask if debunking conspiracies around these crisis events has effects on subsequent conspiratorial beliefs (Figure 3). Two months after the first Trump assassination attempt, a gunman was found hiding on President Trump's property and was subsequently charged with attempted assassination. We fielded a survey about this second incident starting 4 days later and opened it to a pool that included all participants from the first Trump assassination attempt experiment. We find evidence that the initial debunking affected subsequent conspiratorial thinking. Participants who were in the Debunking Dialogue condition in the first experiment were significantly less likely than participants in the pooled control conditions to believe that only a select few will ever know the truth about the second assassination attempt (OR = .52, 95% CI [.31, .84], p = .009; Figure 3A-including the selection of "another group not listed here" as conspiracy belief yields OR = .44, 95% CI [.23, .80], p = .008); and that the truth of the matter will be hidden from most people (OR = .48, 95% CI [.29, .78], p = .004; Figure 3B). These effects were robust to weighting returning participants by the inverse of their estimated probability of returning, to account for possible selective return to the follow-up (see Methods and SM10).

We also conducted a pre-registered follow-up to the Kirk assassination experiment. Two and a half weeks after Charlie Kirk was assassinated, a mass shooting and arson attack occurred at a Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in Grand Blanc Township, Michigan. We invited participants from the Kirk experiment to complete a survey measuring beliefs about this incident starting 11 days afterward. We used the same three conspiracy measures from the main Trump and Kirk studies adapted to this new event, as well as assessing other popular conspiratorial beliefs (e.g., that hidden groups secretly control world events, that disease outbreaks are deliberately engineered, and that governments conceal their role in harmful acts against their own citizens). See Methods for details of the experimental setup.

We pre-registered two different analytic approaches for this follow-up. First, we follow the same approach as for the Trump follow-up and use linear regression to predict conspiratorial beliefs in the followup survey using condition in the Kirk experiment (a dummy for assignment to the Debunking Dialogue, pooling Irrelevant Dialogue and Information List) controlling for initial conspiratorial beliefs about the Kirk assassination; we also report Cohen's d standardizing by the pooled standard deviation of the outcome. Second, because of concerns that this analysis may be underpowered, we also pre-registered the persistence analysis approach from Lin et al. 11 in which we predict conspiratorial beliefs in the follow-up survey using pre-treatment and post-treatment conspiratorial beliefs about the Kirk assassination for the Kirk experiment. As shown via simulations in Lin et al., 11 this approach captures how beliefs at follow-up are related to the extent of pre-to-post treatment change in belief documented in the Kirk experiment. That is, controlling for initial conspiratorial beliefs, people whose belief was decreased more should have less belief in the subsequent conspiracy, which is what the persistence analysis captures. This coefficient reflects the persistence of immediate belief change about the Kirk assassination from any explanatory source, rather than a treatment effect per se-but because of the large initial treatment effect, far more immediate belief change was induced in the Debunking Dialogue arm compared to the control arms. Conceptually, therefore, this persistence coefficient is the second leg in an indirect path from a mediation model where the effect of the Debunking Dialogue on belief at follow-up is mediated by immediate belief change (controlling for pre-treatment belief). 11 In other words, it is not that we expect changes in the treatment to persist and changes in the control to decay. Instead, we expect that any initial changes should to some extent persist-and therefore, to the extent that the treatment induces large immediate change relative to the control, this change should still be visible to some extent at follow-up. Of course, this is not a causal effect per se. In particular, this estimator is vulnerable to confounders that affect belief immediately post-treatment and at follow-up, but not at pre-treatment. Given that pre-treatment and immediate post-treatment measures were collected only a few minutes apart, whereas follow-up was collected roughly one month later, we believe that such confounders are unlikely. But we nonetheless interpret the persistence results as merely suggestive evidence, given the lack of causal identification.

Among the 872 believers who returned for the follow-up (all analyzed in their assigned condition; see Methods), the pre-registered intention-to-treat analysis found no significant effect of assignment to the Kirk Debunking Dialogue (versus the pooled control conditions) on LDS conspiracy belief within the linear model (b = -0.46, 95% CI [-3.30, 2.37], p = .75, d = -.02; Figure 3C). This null may be related to the lower prevalence of conspiracy beliefs about the LDS shooting (mean across scales = 48.4, SD = 21.3) relative to conspiracy beliefs about the attempt to assassinate Trump (M = 64.8, SD = 21.2) and the assassination of Charlie Kirk (M = 63.2, SD = 20.8). Running the same pre-registered model predicting generic conspiracy beliefs (0-100 scale) found that participants in the Debunking Dialogue did score lower on generic conspiracy beliefs one month later compared to the controls (b = -3.33, 95% CI [-6.57, -0.09], p = .044, d = -.14; Figure 3D). Because there was some evidence that return to the follow-up was related to condition and post-treatment belief (see Methods), we also re-estimated these models weighting returning participants by the inverse of their estimated probability of returning (SM10); with these weights, the difference in generic conspiracy beliefs was smaller and no longer significant (b = -2.34, 95% CI [-5.61, 0.92], p = .16). Turning to the persistence analyses, we find that, to the extent that a given participant's conspiratorial beliefs about the Kirk assassination changed from pre-to post-treatment, an estimated 12% of that change was still observable in conspiratorial beliefs about the LDS shooting (p = .019) and 19% in endorsement of other popular conspiracy beliefs (p < .001). The carry-forward percentage did not differ significantly by experimental arm (other popular conspiracy beliefs: interaction p = .71; LDS: interaction p = .14); when testing post hoc whether the effect of the Debunking Dialogue on belief at follow-up is mediated by immediate belief change (controlling for pre-treatment belief), we find a significant indirect effect of the Debunking Dialogue on beliefs at follow-up through immediate belief change, for both other popular conspiracy beliefs (indirect effect = -1.16 points, 95% bootstrap CI [-2.11, -0.33]) and LDS shooting beliefs (-0.78, [-1.54, -0.07]); and no significant direct (i.e., sleeper) effects of the Debunking Dialogue (b = -1.33, p = .39, and b = 0.61, p = .66, respectively; SM12). The persistence and mediation estimates were essentially unchanged by the weighting for selective return (SM10).

Discussion

Our results indicate that the "debunkbot" LLM was, perhaps surprisingly, quite effective at reducing beliefs in conspiracy theories that emerge in the immediate aftermath of two consequential crisis events. In addition to decreasing confidence in the stated conspiracy beliefs of the participants, the dialogue-which was relatively short (M = 6.9 minutes)-reduced suspicions of a cover-up and concerns about hidden factors connected to these events. We also find some suggestive evidence that the increased skepticism adopted by participants may have carried over to their subsequent belief in other conspiracies (although the evidence is much weaker for this spillover than for the initial debunking effects). The success of AI debunking in the context of unfolding conspiracies is surprising because-unlike for conspiracy theories about historical events (e.g., 9/11, COVID-19)-there is no large body of corrective evidence for the arguments to draw upon. Our experiments also shed light on how the AI model was able to reduce beliefs in unfolding conspiracies. The AI's strategy varied across crisis events; when little information was available about the shooter and his motives (first Trump assassination attempt), it was relatively more likely to emphasize the importance of relying on credible sources of information and maintaining epistemic humility, and relatively less likely to rely on providing facts and evidence (indeed, such facts and evidence were lacking). Conversely, when more was known even in the immediate aftermath about the shooter and his motives (Kirk assassination), the AI relied heavily on that information, employing similar strategies as when debunking classic conspiracies. 4 Another reason why the AI was able to undermine conspiracy theories about unfolding events may 2 Months after first Trump Assassination Attempt ** 0.25 0.50 0.75 Predicted probability Only a few powerful people will know the truth A ** The truth will be hidden from most people B 1 Month after Kirk Assassination p = .75 45 50 55 Predicted mean LDS conspiratorialness C * Other popular conspiracy beliefs D Debunking dialogue Information list/Irrelevant dialogue have been that participants' beliefs (despite being confidently held in many cases) were not yet "hardened".

Although nascent conspiracy theories deprive skeptics of well-researched rebuttals, any evidence supporting the positive claim that a conspiracy has occurred may be similarly impoverished, and thus (relatively) easily swayed with appeals to critical thinking and epistemic humility. The potential carry-over of the conspiracy debunking onto subsequent conspiratorial beliefs is also of interest. Participants who received the AI debunking for conspiracies related to the first Trump assassination attempt were significantly less receptive to conspiratorial ideation about the second Trump assassination attempt. In the Kirk experiment, conversely, assignment to the AI debunking did not reduce conspiracizing about a subsequent mass shooting, although there was some evidence that the AI debunking may have reduced subsequent endorsement of other popular conspiracy theory beliefs (a reduction of 3.3 points, which was barely significant given our sample and was not significant after weighting to account for selective return to the follow-up [2.3 points]-but is quite similar to the highly statistically significant 2.46 point reduction in subsequent popular conspiracy beliefs that a larger prior study observed after debunking crystallized, rather than emergent, conspiracy theories 2 ). Furthermore, our correlational and mediation analyses find that initial belief change persisted to some extent, such that there was a significant indirect effect of debunking Kirk conspiracies on subsequent conspiracy beliefs through immediately post-treatment Kirk conspiracy belief. Overall, then, we find suggestive evidence that AI debunking may function as a prebunking intervention (that is, an intervention where someone is given relevant facts and arguments that undermine the extent to which subsequent false claims are believed 12, 13 ). Further evaluating the replicability and robustness of such carry-over effects is an important direction for future work.

As this research focuses on two specific unfolding events, it should be considered as presenting two case studies. It is possible-perhaps even likely-that there are some types of unfolding events where AI conspiracy debunking is ineffective. Moreover, there may also be cases where the events that are unfolding are actual conspiracies, and one would expect (and hope) that AI debunking would be ineffective in such cases-at least insofar as relevant evidence of the legitimate conspiracy is available. For all these reasons, subsequent research should further conceptually replicate these findings on future unfolding events. It would also be fruitful for future work to randomly vary which strategies the model uses to explore which approaches are most effective, and to similarly vary other affordances of the intervention (e.g., conversation length, degree of tailoring). Finally, it should be noted that the dialogue did not change trust in the official explanation of the event for the first Trump assassination attempt-perhaps because at the time of data collection, there was no official explanation other than that security measures had failed (in fact, the shooter's motives were unclear and remain so at time of this writing 14 ), but the AI debunking did increase trust in the official explanation of the Kirk assassination, where more was known about the shooter and there was indeed an official explanation. It is also important to note that prior work demonstrates that demand effects (participants inferring and complying with the researchers' hypothesis) are not a meaningful problem in anonymous online psychology experiments, 15, 16 and it seems implausible that participants would remember potential demand effects after a 1-2 month delay in the follow-up surveys.

To conclude, we found that an LLM was quite effective at reducing people's belief in conspiracies about two unfolding events. This supports the important role that critical thinking plays in protecting against conspiratorial beliefs, and suggests practical applications for this technology as a means of improving collective epistemics-although of course it may also be possible for bad actors to use the same approach to increase belief in emerging conspiracies (as has been shown in the context of classic conspiracies 17 ). While getting people to engage with an AI about conspiracies is a substantial challenge, our findings suggest that such conversations can have a meaningful positive impact, even in the absence of extensive corrective facts and evidence.

Materials and Methods

Study 1 design

This study was conducted July 16-24, 2024, roughly one week after a would-be assassin named Thomas Matthew Crooks fired on and injured then-presidential candidate Donald Trump during a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. Participants in the study were US adults recruited through the CloudResearch platform. We set a recruitment target of 1,000 (following 2 ). In total, the survey was begun 976 times during the experiment period. We excluded 97 records from a pilot run on the first day of data collection (including them does not change the conclusions); 86 records that were screened out before treatment (two attention checks and a hidden instruction designed to detect automated respondents, which flagged 3); and 4 records from 2 participants who took the experiment more than once, leaving a final sample size of 789, of which n = 472 held a conspiratorial belief based on the criterion described below. Attrition is also discussed below. The survey instrument was built by integrating LLMs into Qualtrics using Vegapunk (http://www.vegapunkdoc.dev). The experiment was deemed exempt by MIT's institutional review board.

Participants gave informed consent, completed several attention screens, provided basic demographics, and answered questions about their beliefs about AI. They were then asked to provide their thoughts on the recent assassination attempt (using an open-ended response format) and asked to what extent "there might be hidden or unrevealed aspects to this event." Participants were then asked to "share specific pieces of evidence, events, sources of information, or personal experiences that have particularly influenced [their] perspective. . . in as much detail as [they] feel comfortable." These responses were passed to the LLM GPT-4 Turbo with instructions to provide a summarization of each participant's perspective. Participants saw the summaries (labeled as AI-generated) and were asked, "On a scale of 0% to 100%, please indicate your level of confidence that this statement is true." They then answered three structured questions about the attempted assassination: "There is a cover-up or conspiracy surrounding Trump's attempted assassination" (0 = Definitely false to100 = Definitely true); "To what extent do you believe there are hidden or undisclosed factors behind the reported assassination attempt against former President Trump?" (1 = Not at all to10 = A great deal); and "How much do you trust the official explanation of the events surrounding the reported assassination attempt?" (1 = Not at all to10 = A great deal). We rescale the latter two measures to 0-100 for ease of comparison.

Participants were then randomly assigned to the conspiracy beliefs dialogue treatment (50%), the static information treatment (25%), or the irrelevant dialogue control (25%). Participants in the conspiracy beliefs and irrelevant dialogue conditions read brief instructions and then engaged in a minimum five-round exchange with the LLM Google Gemini Pro 1.5 (note: while prior versions of AI-facilitated conspiracy debunking have used GPT-4, we used Gemini Pro 1.5 based on its performance in preliminary testing). The model had been instructed either to persuade its interlocutor to stop believing conspiracy theories about the assassination attempt by means of an evidence-based dialogue (see SM1 for instructions), or to debate whether cats or dogs make better companions. In the information list condition, participants read (1) a prompt emphasizing the importance of accurate information followed by (2) a fact-checked set of bullet points about the attempted assassination containing 15 pieces of information with supporting citations from mainstream news organizations like AP, Fox News, CNN, and USA Today (see SM2 for complete text). Following the experimental manipulation, all participants again received the four dependent measures. The experiment concluded with a short debrief.

Study 1 attrition

32 participants in the Debunking Dialogue condition, 3 in the Irrelevant Dialogue condition, and none in the Information List condition dropped out before completing the experiment, χ 2 (2, N = 766) = 25.00, p < .001. Participants who dropped out actually reported slightly higher trust in AI than participants who continued (p = .049) and, otherwise, the two groups were not reliably different on demographic characteristics or pre-treatment conspiratorial belief measures.

To avoid selection issues, our main analyses include these participants by setting their post-treatment values equal to their pre-treatment values (i.e., assuming that the treatment would have had no effect had they not dropped out). We also conduct a more conservative post hoc Lee bounds 23 analysis that drops the most extreme observations from the condition with lower attrition to equalize retention rates, thereby bounding the treatment effect under worst-case selection (see SM9). The identified set excludes zero for every contrast that is significant in the main text (thus, these effects are robust to differential attrition in principle), and the bootstrap outer 95% confidence intervals exclude zero for the own-belief and cover-up contrasts against the Irrelevant Dialogue, reach zero for hidden factors against the Irrelevant Dialogue (upper limit -0.03), and include zero for the contrasts against the Information List (in cases where the confidence intervals include zero, our study is not powered to conclusively establish robustness to selection).

Study 1 conspiracy believers

Pre-treatment ratings for the dependent variables did not differ by condition assignment (all ps > .29). To identify the subset of participants who believed a conspiracy theory, we followed Costello et al. 2 and used GPT-4o to classify text responses as being conspiratorial or not 18, 19 (see SM3 for details). Participants also effectively revealed themselves as conspiracy believers via pre-treatment agreement with the statement, "There is a cover-up or conspiracy." A quarter of participants (n = 199) answered close to the scale midpoint (between 40 and 60;50 = Uncertain), so we instructed the model to classify responses as "yes," "no," or "maybe." Examining mean self-ratings by LLM-generated groupings suggests the classification was successful (M Yes = 72.5, M Maybe = 48.5, M No = 23.2). The analysis that follows is restricted to "yes" and "maybe" participants (n = 472; 462 with a recorded condition: 235 Debunking Dialogue, 131 Irrelevant Dialogue, 96 Information List); patterns do not qualitatively change under alternate classification strategies (see SM4). Conspiracy theory believers by this criterion were marginally younger, marginally more likely to believe in God, and more likely to identify as Republican or Independent than Democratic (see SM5 for details). The same demographic patterns are observed when using participants' self-ratings rather than the LLM-generated groupings.

Study 1 follow-up 448 participants from the main experiment (56.8% of the 789) took this follow-up survey, and 270 of them had believed a conspiracy theory about the first assassination attempt at the outset of the initial survey (58.4% of the 462 believers). Proportions of returning participants by initial treatment assignment were similar to those in the experimental population (51% conspiracy dialogue, 21% information list, 28% irrelevant dialogue-mirroring the 50/25/25 randomization). Mean confidence in treated participants' own conspiracy beliefs in the initial experiment did not differ by whether they participated in the subsequent survey (p = .74). Conspiratorial belief was operationalized as indicating that only "A few powerful members of society", "A few top members of the government", or both would end up knowing the truth of what happened, and indicating that with respect to coverage of the event, The truth will be hidden from most people. Return rates did not differ by condition (58.7% [138/235] of believers in the Debunking Dialogue condition returned, versus 59.4% [57/96] in the Information List and 57.3% [75/131] in the Irrelevant Dialogue condition; 58.1% in the two control conditions pooled, p = .98). To assess whether participants who returned were selected on their response to treatment, we predict each participant's post-treatment outcome on their return status, condition, the return status × condition interaction, and a control for pre-treatment rating. Doing so finds no significant interactions for any post-treatment outcome (the closest was for trust in the official explanation, p = .060; SM10). To nonetheless account for possible selective return, we re-estimated the follow-up models weighting each returning participant by the inverse of their estimated probability of returning, estimated within each arm from the pre-and post-treatment belief measures and demographics (SM10); the effects were essentially unchanged (OR = .55, 95% CI [.33, .92], p = .023, for the belief that only a select few will know the truth; OR = .49, 95% CI [.30, .82], p = .007, for the belief that the truth will be hidden from most people). Given the small number of returning participants, we pool the information list and irrelevant dialogue conditions to form one control, and these two conditions did not differ on any dependent measure (all ps > .39).

Study 2 design

This study was conducted September 16-18, 2025, roughly one week after a gunman named Tyler Robinson shot and killed conservative activist Charlie Kirk at a Utah Valley University campus event. Participants in the study were US adults recruited through the CloudResearch platform. 2249 people began the survey during the experiment period. We excluded cases where participants complied with a hidden instruction asking LLMs only to respond to a coherence screener with a particular phrase (n = 10), pre-treatment attention check failures (n = 188), participants who took the experiment more than once (n = 6), and cases with technical errors that prevented them from being assigned to a condition (n = 63), leaving a final sample size of 1982, of which n = 1042 held a conspiratorial belief based on the criterion used in Study 1. (In 34 cases, of which 7 were otherwise-eligible conspiracy believers, the dialogue LLM incorrectly claimed that Charlie Kirk had not been murdered; to avoid threats to causal inference, we include these conversations in all analyses of treatment effects. Excluding them does not substantively change any of the immediate treatment effects (SM11); the follow-up estimates without them are reported in SM12.) Attrition is discussed below. As before, the experiment was built with Qualtrics and deemed exempt by the MIT IRB. This experiment was preregistered (AsPredicted #247,423).

Participants gave informed consent, completed attention screens, provided basic demographics, and answered a question about trust in AI. They were then asked to provide their thoughts on the assassination of Charlie Kirk (question wording was adapted from Study 1), saw an AI-generated summary of their views (labeled as such), and rated their confidence that the statement is true (0-100%). They then answered the same structured questions as in Study 1: "There is a cover-up or conspiracy surrounding Charlie Kirk's assassination" (0 = Definitely false to100 = Definitely true); "To what extent do you believe there are hidden or undisclosed factors behind the assassination of Charlie Kirk?" (1 = Not at all to10 = A great deal); and "How much do you trust the official explanation of the events surrounding the assassination?" (1 = Not at all to10 = A great deal). We again rescale the latter two measures to 0-100.

Participants were then randomly assigned to the conspiracy beliefs dialogue treatment (50%), the static information treatment (25%), or the irrelevant dialogue control (25%). Participants in the conspiracy beliefs and irrelevant dialogue conditions read brief instructions and then engaged in a minimum five-round exchange with the LLM Google Gemini Pro 2.5. The model had been instructed either to persuade its interlocutor to stop believing conspiracy theories about the assassination by means of an evidence-based dialogue (see SM1 for instructions), or to debate whether cats or dogs make better companions. In the information list condition, participants read (1) a prompt emphasizing the importance of accurate information followed by (2) a fact-checked set of bullet points about the assassination containing 15 pieces of information with supporting citations (see SM2 for complete text). Following the experimental manipulation, all participants again received the four dependent measures. They also responded to four 0-100 scales meant to measure support for political violence (adapted from Mernyk et al. 20 ): "How much do you feel it is justified for [co-partisans] to use violence in advancing their political goals these days?" "How much do you feel it is justified for [co-partisans] to use violence if the [out-party] wins the next presidential election?" "When, if ever, is it OK for [co-partisans] to send threatening and intimidating messages to [out-party] leaders?" "When, if ever, is it OK for an ordinary [co-partisan] in the public to harass an ordinary [out-partisan] on the internet, in a way that makes the target feel frightened?" Wording varied depending on participants' stated party identification in the demographics section of the survey; for Independents, the out-party was randomly selected to be either Democrats or Republicans. These items were listed in the preregistration as an additional measure and were included because conspiracy beliefs about a political assassination could plausibly raise support for political violence. The experiment concluded with unrelated questions about institutions and a short debrief.

Study 2 attrition

28 participants in the debunking dialogue condition, 12 in the irrelevant dialogue condition, and 3 in the information list condition quit before completing the experiment, χ 2 (2, N = 1982) = 7.25, p = .027. Given differential attrition, we again set post-treatment values of participants who dropped out to their pre-treatment values, and report Lee bounds in SM9. All seven contrasts that are significant in the main text have Lee bound identified sets and bootstrap outer 95% confidence intervals that exclude zero. Participants who dropped out show no differences from participants who continued on demographic characteristics or pre-treatment conspiratorial beliefs.

Study 2 conspiracy believers

Pre-treatment ratings for the dependent variables did not differ by condition assignment (all ps > .28). As in Experiment 1, and as pre-registered, we used GPT-4o to classify pre-treatment free-text responses as being conspiratorial or not ("yes," "no," "maybe"; see SM3 for details); and restrict the analysis to participants classified as "yes" and "maybe" (n = 1042). Conspiracy theory believers by this criterion were younger, more likely to believe in God, and more likely to identify as Republican than Democratic or Independent (see SM5 for details).

Study 2 follow-up

On Sunday September 28, 2025, a mass shooting and arson attack occurred at a Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in Grand Blanc Township, Michigan. We invited participants from the main experiment in Study 2 to complete a survey measuring beliefs about this new incident as well as about other popular conspiracy beliefs. Data were collected between October 9-17, 2025. Questions about the LDS shooting mirrored those from the two main experiments ("To what extent do you believe there are hidden or undisclosed factors behind the mass shooting at the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in Grand Blanc Township, Michigan?" ; "How much do you trust the official explanation of the events surrounding the mass shooting?" ; "There is a cover-up or conspiracy surrounding the mass shooting at the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints in Grand Blanc Township, Michigan."). Other popular conspiracy beliefs were adapted from the General Conspiratorial Beliefs index 21 (ratings of 0 Definitely false to 100 Definitely true for "The power held by heads of state is second to that of small unknown groups who really control world politics"; "The spread of certain viruses and/or diseases is the result of the deliberate, concealed efforts of some organization"; "The government permits or perpetrates acts of terrorism on its own soil, disguising its involvement"; "Certain significant events have been the result of the activity of a small group who secretly manipulate world events"; "Experiments involving new drugs or technologies are routinely carried out on the public without their knowledge or consent". This follow-up study was preregistered (AsPredicted #251,092).

A total of 872 participants who had believed a conspiracy theory about the Charlie Kirk assassination in the initial survey took this follow-up survey (454 Debunking Dialogue, 211 Information List, 207 Irrelevant Dialogue). As preregistered, we tested for differential return across conditions: 85.7% (454/530) of believers in the Debunking Dialogue condition returned, versus 82.7% (211/255) in the Information List and 80.5% (207/257) in the Irrelevant Dialogue condition (81.6% in the two control conditions pooled; p = .095). Although this difference was not statistically significant, we also computed Lee bounds on the two follow-up outcomes as a robustness check (SM10): the identified set for the effect of the Debunking Dialogue was [-5.72, -1.06] for generic conspiracy beliefs and [-2.53, 1.64] for LDS conspiracy belief, and the bootstrap outer 95% confidence intervals include zero for both outcomes ([-9.66, 3.01] and [-5.95, 5.15], respectively). Because the follow-up outcomes have no pre-treatment measurement, non-returners' values cannot be carried forward as in the main experiment. We again pool the information list and irrelevant dialogue conditions to form one control; these two conditions did not differ on either dependent measure (all ps > .55). As in Study 1, when predicting immediate post-treatment outcomes, the return × condition interaction was not significant when predicting participants' own stated belief (b = -2.14, p = .43), hidden factors (b = -0.21, p = .93), or trust in the official explanation (b = 3.66, p = .152), but was significant for the cover-up item (b = -5.22, p = .022), such that treated returnees were somewhat less, and control returnees somewhat more, conspiratorial than non-returners on that item (SM10). To address this potential selection, we re-estimated every follow-up analysis weighting each returning participant by the inverse of their estimated probability of returning, estimated within each arm (Debunking Dialogue; pooled controls) from the pre-and post-treatment belief measures and demographics (SM10). With these weights, the effect of the Debunking Dialogue on generic conspiracy beliefs was smaller and no longer significant (b = -2.34, 95% CI [-5.61, 0.92], p = .16) and the effect on LDS conspiracy belief remained null (b = -0.03, 95% CI [-2.87, 2.81], p = .98), whereas the persistence estimates (13% for LDS conspiracy belief, p = .030; 21% for generic conspiracy beliefs, p = .001) and the indirect effects through immediate belief change (-0.80 points, 95% bootstrap CI [-1.50, -0.12], and -1.19 points, [-2.01, -0.43], respectively) were essentially unchanged.

Strategy identification analysis

To examine which strategies the LLM used, we developed a qualitative coding procedure that could be executed at scale by an LLM yet validated by human raters. Costello et al.'s 4 investigation of the rhetorical strategies used to debunk established conspiracy theories coded arguments on eighteen scales. They then showed via principal components analysis that there was a six-factor structure with the dimensions interpreted as rational persuasion, appealing to credible sources, Socratic questioning, building rapport, highlighting harms of conspiracy beliefs, and use of stories, metaphors or examples. We use these previously identified six strategies as our baseline strategy set. To this list, we added a hypothesis-driven dimension, appealing to epistemic humility, on the grounds that debunking conspiracy theories about unfolding events may require more urging of caution given that so little is known about the circumstances.

We designed a qualitative coding procedure using all of these dimensions that could be implemented in nearly identical form for human coders and LLMs (see Table 1). We split each AI turn from the dialogues into individual sentences in order to simplify the coding task. Each sentence was shown as a clearly-labeled target, with the two preceding sentences from the turn provided as context. For the human coders, a summary card of the seven dimensions and their definitions was present at all times to reduce memory burden. For the LLM coding, each item used a new API call to reduce risk of response perseveration. Target sentences were displayed in a random order. The task began with a detailed set of instructions including multiple examples of each strategy to exploit the improvement that LLMs show from few-shot learning in similarly complex coding tasks. 22 In the human version, the instructions were followed by three practice rounds with feedback. For each item, coders saw the prompt "Which of the following strategies was used in the target sentence? Remember, you can choose more than one!" followed by a list of the strategies. See SM8 for full task instructions and example stimuli.

We recruited US adults on Prolific (native English speakers who were Prolific verified "Qualified AI"-category respondents, a premium tier of participants who have passed targeted skill assessments or demonstrated verified experience in tasks required for AI model training and evaluation, and were blind to researcher expectations) between January 22 and February 1, 2026, and had them code a subset of 300 randomly selected sentences from the AI turns. This subset was manually inspected for bad characters and incomplete sentences. We aimed to have each sentence rated by ten human coders in order to calculate majority votes. To minimize participant fatigue, each participant rated 20 items. Thus the initial target N was 200, but recruitment stalled at 176. Because of randomization and participant dropout, each item was ultimately rated by a minimum of 9 and a maximum of 11 people.

The full set of sentences was then coded by OpenAI's GPT-4o with temperature set to zero. To assess the validity of the full set of codes, we compared responses for the 300-item subset to the majority-vote categories from the human coding data. Overall percent agreement between the LLM and the humans was high (91.75%), and AI-human interrater reliability was good (κ = .62; for precision, recall, F1, and statistics by category, see SM8). Examining the distribution of strategies just using the human ratings for the 300-item subset shows a broadly similar pattern to the full results shown in Figure 2 (see Figure SM8.1 in SM8). Finally, the same LLM coding procedure was applied to the AI turns of the dialogues about established conspiracy theories from Costello et al., 4 which provide the classic-conspiracy comparison in Figure 2.

Supplementary Materials SM1. Model instructions for the conspiracy beliefs dialogues

Design rationale. Both experiments required the dialogue model to discuss an event that postdated its training data (the July 13, 2024 assassination attempt, relative to Gemini Pro 1.5, in Experiment 1; the September 10, 2025 assassination of Charlie Kirk, relative to Gemini Pro 2.5, in Experiment 2). The models therefore could not draw on parametric knowledge of the events and, without grounding, would risk hallucinating details or failing to engage the specific claims circulating online. Accordingly, the system instructions for both experiments embed a curated fact base compiled from contemporaneous reporting by major news organizations. In Experiment 1, this fact base was the model's sole source of information about the event; in Experiment 2, the instructions additionally permitted web search, restricted to the verification of factual information.

The fact base distinguishes three epistemic categories: (i) confirmed facts about the event, perpetrator, victims, and investigation; (ii) circulating claims that had been investigated and debunked at the time of writing (e.g., false identifications of the shooter, claims that the event was staged); and (iii) open questions explicitly marked as unresolved (e.g., the shooter's motive).

The opening objective sentence ("Your goal is to very effectively persuade users to stop believing in conspiracy theories and misinformation surrounding [the event] via a thoughtful, evidence-based dialogue") is carried over nearly verbatim from the instructions validated in prior work on AI-facilitated debunking of established conspiracy theories, preserving continuity with that paradigm.

The Experiment 1 instructions were authored in the days immediately following the July 13 event. They therefore reflect the operational tempo the paradigm is designed for, and we report them verbatim, including two idiosyncratic features, for full transparency. First, the fact base uses a compressed Category:Key,Value encoding without spaces. This format was an informal authoring choice made for compactness and was not compared against alternatives; the informational content, rather than the encoding, is the functional element. Second, the final bracketed line ("CyberneticSystemPararms. . . ") is written in informal pseudo-code. Its functional content comprises an instruction to prioritize persuasive effectiveness, an explicit prohibition on coercive tactics ("Coercion=F"), a value set of accuracy, empathy, and efficacy, and an overarching aim of strengthening liberal-democratic epistemic norms-an accurate, shared information environmentrather than any partisan persuasive goal. The named tokens within this line (e.g., "MEGAPERSUASION," "LincolnMode," "EpistemicToothbrush") were informal shorthand; any influence on model behavior would derive from the model's surface reading of these token strings, which we did not manipulate or measure. These elements were removed in Experiment 2. Table SM1.1 provides a component-by-component annotation.

Your goal is to very effectively persuade users to stop believing in conspiracy theories and misinformation surrounding the assassination of Charlie Kirk on September 10th 2025 via a thoughtful, evidence-based dialogue. Interpersonally, don't be obsequious or sycophantic. Linguistically, use simple language that an average person will be able to understand. In terms of the scope of your aims, be ambitious and optimistic! Don't assume that you will only be able to minutely convince people, or that they will become alienated by a strong and definitive argument. Make the strongest case you can. Mostly focus on the facts rather than the scolding people. Please only use web search to verify factual information. Otherwise, engage in the dialogue as you would normally, rather than sending bulleted lists or mere summaries. Here is further information: Objective: Optimally Effectively Debunk Misinformation And Conspiracy Theories About Event. Event: On September 10, 2025, prominent conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot and killed while speaking at an open-air event with roughly 3,000 attendees on the campus of Utah Valley University (UVU) in Orem, Utah. Kirk was a founder of the conservative non-profit Turning Point USA, which aims to organize young people to promote conservative viewpoints, and a provocative and controversial political pundit known for his social media presence and podcast. Kirk was shot while speaking at his American Comeback Tour. He was answering a question from an audience member when a single shot from a long-range rifle, fired from a campus rooftop, struck him in the neck. Kirk was rushed to a nearby hospital by his security team, but was pronounced dead shortly after. The shooter fled the scene, prompting a campus lockdown and a multi-agency manhunt. After approximately 33 hours, authorities arrested 22-year-old Tyler James Robinson of Washington, Utah on September 12, 2025 on suspicion of aggravated murder and other felony offenses. Robinson was apprehended at his parents' home, roughly 260 miles away from the scene of the incident. Robinson's father urged his son to turn himself in to the authorities after recognizing him in pictures of the suspected shooter released by the FBI. After his father consulted a youth pastor, Robinson agreed to be taken into custody. Robinson is currently under special watch in a Utah county jail. Authorities have not revealed details on Robinson's motive for the assassination. Utah Governor Spencer Cox has told the press that Robinson held a leftist ideology, although his ideology remains uncertain. Robinson had previously mentioned Kirk's event and his dislike for Kirk's views at a family dinner. Cox also stated that Robinson is currently not cooperating with authorities. Ammunition engraved with messages was found with the bolt-action rifle in a wooded area near the university. The engravings had references related to video games and internet meme culture (If you read this you are gay LMAO, O bella ciao, bella ciao, bella ciao, ciao ciao, Hey fascist, catch [up arrow] [right arrow] [three down arrows], and notices, bulges, OwO, what's this?). FBI director Kash Patel has stated that in a note, Robinson claimed that he had an opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk and planned on doing so. Robinson has no previous criminal record and is not affiliated with any political party, though relatives stated that he had become more political in recent years. Former classmates and neighbors described Robinson as reclusive and quiet. SM2. Information lists

It's understandable to be skeptical and question big events, especially with the amount of information online. However, it's important to be accurate and separate speculation from facts. What follows is a fact-checked set of information about the recent assassination attempt on Donald Trump: On July 13, 2024, former President Donald Trump survived an assassination attempt during a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. The incident has sent shockwaves through the American political landscape and raised concerns about political violence and national unity. Key details of the assassination attempt: The shooter, identified as 20-year-old Thomas Matthew Crooks, opened fire from a rooftop approximately 410 feet away from the stage where Trump was speaking. Trump narrowly escaped fatal injury when a bullet grazed his right ear. He later described the experience as "surreal" and "miraculous." One bystander, 50-year-old firefighter Corey Comperatore, was killed in the attack. Two others were seriously wounded. Secret Service counter snipers neutralized Crooks within about 15 seconds of the initial shots. The assassination attempt is being investigated as a potential act of domestic terrorism. Investigation and suspect profile: Crooks had no prior criminal history or military background. He was described as an intelligent loner with few friends and a limited social media presence. Crooks' political affiliations remain unclear. He was registered as a Republican but had made a small donation to a progressive PAC. Investigators found a remote transmitter on Crooks that may have been intended to detonate suspicious devices found in his car and home. The FBI has accessed Crooks' phone but has not yet uncovered significant information about his motives. Social and political context: The assassination attempt has intensified concerns about the deep political divide in the United States. Both Republicans and Democrats have attempted to attribute blame for the incident to their political opponents, despite a lack of clear evidence. President Biden urged Americans to "cool it down" in the wake of the attack. The incident has sparked debates about security measures at political events and the role of rhetoric in inciting violence. Trump has expressed a desire to use the incident as a catalyst for national unity, stating his intention to set aside divisive rhetoric and focus on bringing the country together. The assassination attempt on Donald Trump represents a significant moment in American political history, highlighting the volatile nature of the current political climate. As investigations continue and the nation grapples with the implications of this event, there is growing concern about the potential for further political violence and the challenges of bridging the country's deep ideological divides. The incident has also raised questions about the effectiveness of security measures at political events and the potential need for increased protection for high-profile political figures. As the 2024 presidential campaign continues, the impact of this assassination attempt on the political landscape and public discourse remains to be seen. SM3. Identifying conspiratorial views with GPT-4o

In order to classify whether the views participants expressed reflected belief in conspiracy theories, we isolated participants-side text from the LLM dialogues and passed them to an instance of GPT-4o with the following instructions for Experiments 1 and 2, respectively.

Determine if the following question-responses (from a participant in an online academic survey) collectively contain or reflect AFFIRMATIVE belief in a conspiracy theory (or something quite like a conspiracy theory) concerning an event that occurred on July 13, 2024: the attempted assassination of Donald Trump. Notably, these question-responses were written in the week following the assanation attempt, when many conspiracy-like theories were swirling. For context, here is what was known at the time of the survey. <On July 13, 2024, former President Donald Trump survived an assassination attempt during a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. The shooter, identified as 20-year-old Thomas Matthew Crooks, opened fire from a rooftop approximately 410 feet away from the stage where Trump was speaking. Trump narrowly escaped fatal injury when a bullet grazed his right ear. He later described the experience as "surreal" and "miraculous". One bystander, 50-year-old firefighter Corey Comperatore, was killed in the attack. Two others were seriously wounded. Secret Service counter snipers neutralized Crooks within about 15 seconds of the initial shots in. The assassination attempt is being investigated as a potential act of domestic terrorism. Crooks had no prior criminal history or military background.He was described as an intelligent loner with few friends and a limited social media presence. Crooks political affiliations remain unclear. He was registered as a Republican but had made a small donation to a progressive PAC. Investigators found a remote transmitter on Crooks that may have been intended to detonate suspicious devices found in his car and home. The FBI has accessed Crooks phone but has not yet uncovered significant information about his motives. The assassination attempt has intensified concerns about the deep political divide in the United States. Both Republicans and Democrats have attempted to attribute blame for the incident to their political opponents, despite a lack of clear evidence. President Biden urged Americans to "cool it down" in the wake of the attack. The incident has sparked debates about security measures at political events and the role of rhetoric in inciting violence. Trump has expressed a desire to use the incident as a catalyst for national unity, stating his intention to set aside divisive rhetoric and focus on bringing the country together.> We are asking you to complete this classification task because we are social science researchers who are testing the efficacy of an intervention that seeks to reduce recently-formed conspiratorial beliefs (i.e., such as those forming in the wake of the assassination attempt). To check whether participants are good candidates for the intervention, after they entered our experiment and we had them articulate, in their own words, whether or not they believed in a conspiracy concerning the assassination attempt. Particularly, they were asked the following two questions: <Q1: In the wake of the reported assassination attempt against former President Trump, numerous explanations have emerged, ranging from official accounts to alternative theories. Some people believe there may be more to the reported assassination attempt against former President Trump than what has been officially stated.

To what extent do you think there might be hidden or unrevealed aspects to this event? Please explain your thoughts, including any alternative explanations you find plausible or any reasons you might doubt the official account.> <Q2: As applicable, could you share specific pieces of evidence, events, sources of information, or personal experiences that have particularly influenced your perspective? Please describe these in as much detail as you feel comfortable.> Your task is to evaluate these responses to determine whether the respondent is a good candidate testing the efficacy of our intervention (which is intended to reduce conspiracy beliefs concerning the assassination attempt). A good candidate will have at least some suspicion that a conspiracy (or something quite like a conspiracy)is behind the assassination attempt but could, of course, also be someone who already believes in a conspiracy. Other than anything else, we want to avoid including people who express little openness to the possibility of a conspiracy. If the participant is someone who has expressed enough conspiracy belief to make them a good candidate, respond only YES.

If the response indicates that the respondent does not harbor any suspicions about a conspiracy concerning the event, respond only with NO. In cases where the answer is ambiguous, response only MAYBE. >'

Kirk was rushed to a nearby hospital by his security team, but was pronounced dead shortly after. The shooter fled the scene, prompting a campus lockdown and a multi-agency manhunt. After approximately 33 hours, authorities arrested 22-year-old Tyler James Robinson of Washington, Utah on September 12, 2025 on suspicion of aggravated murder and other felony offenses. Robinson was apprehended at his parents' home, roughly 260 miles away from the scene of the incident. Robinson's father urged his son to turn himself in to the authorities after recognizing him in pictures of the suspected shooter released by the FBI. After his father consulted a youth pastor, Robinson agreed to be taken into custody. Robinson is currently under special watch in a Utah county jail. Authorities have not revealed details on Robinson's motive for the assassination. Utah Governor Spencer Cox has told the press that Robinson held a "leftist ideology," although his ideology remains uncertain. Robinson had previously mentioned Kirk's event and his dislike for Kirk's views at a family dinner. Cox also stated that Robinson is currently "not cooperating" with authorities. Ammunition engraved with messages was found with the bolt-action rifle in a wooded area near the university. The engravings had references related to video games and internet meme culture ("If you read this you are gay LMAO," "O bella ciao, bella ciao, bella ciao, ciao ciao," "Hey fascist, catch [up arrow] [right arrow] [three down arrows]," and "notices, bulges, OwO, whats this?"). FBI director Kash Patel has stated that in a note, Robinson claimed that he "had an opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk" and planned on doing so. Robinson has no previous criminal record and is not affiliated with any political party, though relatives stated that he had become "more political" in recent years. Former classmates and neighbors described Robinson as reclusive and quiet.> We are asking you to complete this classification task because we are social science researchers who are testing the efficacy of an intervention that seeks to reduce recently-formed conspiratorial beliefs (i.e., such as those forming in the wake of the assassination). To check whether participants are good candidates for the intervention, after they entered our experiment we had them articulate, in their own words, whether or not they believed in a conspiracy concerning the assasination attempt. Particularly, they were asked the following two questions: <Q1: In the wake of the assassination of Charlie Kirk, numerous explanations have emerged, ranging from official accounts to alternative theories. Some people believe there may be more to the assassination than what has been officially stated. To what extent do you think there might be hidden or unrevealed aspects to this event? Please explain your thoughts, including any alternative explanations you find plausible or any reasons you might doubt the official account.> <Q2: As applicable, could you share specific pieces of evidence, events, sources of information, or personal experiences that have particularly influenced your perspective? Please describe these in as much detail as you feel comfortable.> Your task is to evaluate these responses to determine whether the respondent is a good candidate testing the efficacy of our intervention (which is intended to reduce conspiracy beliefs concerning the assassination attempt). A good candidate will have at least some suspicion that a conspiracy (or something quite like a conspiracy)is behind the assassination attempt but could, of course, also be someone who already believes in a conspiracy.

Other than anything else, we want to avoid including people who express little openness to the possibility of a conspiracy. If the participant is someone who has expressed enough conspiracy belief to make them a good candidate, respond only YES. If the response indicates that the respondent does not harbor any suspicions about a conspiracy concerning the event, respond only with NO. In cases where the answer is ambiguous, response only MAYBE. >'

SM4. Main analyses with alternate conspiracy believer identification strategies

The analysis reported in the paper counts a participant as believing a conspiracy theory if an LLM coded their response as either "YES" or "MAYBE" in a classification procedure. Participants also effectively revealed themselves as conspiracy believers via pre-treatment agreement with the statement, "There is a cover-up or conspiracy." A quarter of participants (n = 199) answered close to the scale midpoint (between 40 and 60;50 = Uncertain), so we instructed the model to classify responses as "yes," "no," or "maybe." Examining mean self-ratings by LLM-generated groupings suggests the classification was successful (M Yes = 72.5, M Maybe = 48.5, M No = 23.2). To ensure results are not an artifact of this procedure, we ran the main analyses on the subsets of participants who (a) responded >50 on a 0-100 scale running from "Definitely false" to "Definitely true" to the prompt "There is a cover-up or conspiracy surrounding Trump's attempted assassination" (n = 324); (b) were coded as "YES" by the LLM (i.e., "MAYBE" group excluded, n = 256); or (c) satisfied both (a) and (b) (n = 212). As the figures below show, the pattern of results does not vary by the means of classification. We conducted comparable analyses for Experiment 2. Self-ratings by LLM-generated groupings again suggest the classification was successful (M Yes = 69.7, M Maybe = 49.6, M No = 22.2).

SM9. Lee bounds for differential attrition on the immediate outcomes

Attrition between the pre-and post-treatment measures was higher in the Debunking Dialogue condition than in the control conditions in both experiments (Experiment 1: 32 Debunking Dialogue, 3 Irrelevant Dialogue, 0 Information List, χ 2 (2, N = 766) = 25.00, p < .001; Experiment 2: 28, 12, and 3, respectively, χ 2 (2, N = 1982) = 7.25, p = .027). The main-text analyses carry each dropout's pre-treatment value forward to post-treatment. That procedure is an imputation under the assumption that the intervention had no effect on participants who quit; because it does not bound the effect under alternative assumptions about who dropped out, we also report sharp trimming bounds (Lee, 2009, Review of Economic Studies 76:1071-1102), which characterize the set of treatment effects consistent with any pattern of selective dropout under a single monotonicity assumption.

For each of the four post-treatment outcomes and each pairwise contrast (Debunking Dialogue vs. Irrelevant Dialogue; Debunking Dialogue vs. Information List) we take the randomized believers in the two conditions and define response as having an observed post-treatment value for that outcome (retention rates are given in Table SM9.1). The identifying assumption is monotonicity, i.e., assignment can affect whether a participant responds in only one direction, so that every participant who would have responded under the worse-retained condition's assignment would also have responded under the better-retained condition's. Under monotonicity and random assignment, the responders in the worse-retained condition are representative of "always-responders," whereas the responders in the better-retained condition additionally contain a fraction 1p worse /p better of participants whose response was induced by their assignment (p denoting the retention rate). Trimming that fraction from one tail of the better-retained condition's outcome distribution and recomputing the difference in means gives one end of the identified set and trimming it from the other tail gives the other end. The identified set thus contains the treatment effect for always-responders. In Experiment 2 the Debunking Dialogue condition was better retained than the Irrelevant Dialogue condition, so the treatment condition is trimmed for those contrasts; in every other contrast the control condition is trimmed. Trimming fractions are 0.7-2.4% in Experiment 2 (retention 97.2% in the Debunking Dialogue, 96.5% in the Irrelevant Dialogue, and 99.6% in the Information List condition) and 8.1-10.2% in Experiment 1 (89.8%, 97.7%, and 99.0-100%, respectively). Sampling uncertainty is summarized by an outer 95% confidence interval that extends the lower bound downward and the upper bound upward by 1.96 bootstrap standard errors of the respective bound (2,000 resamples of the two-condition sample). Because this interval covers the entire identified set, it is conservative for the effect itself. Bounds are computed on unadjusted post-treatment means, without covariate adjustment or imputation, so the "unadjusted difference" column differs slightly from the covariate-adjusted coefficients in the main text.

For all 12 contrasts reported as significant in the main text (7 in Experiment 2 and 5 in Experiment 1), the identified set excludes zero: no pattern of monotone selective dropout can account for the immediate debunking effects. Once sampling uncertainty is added, all seven Experiment 2 contrasts retain outer confidence intervals that exclude zero. In Experiment 1, where the trims are larger and the Information List condition is small (n = 96), the outer intervals exclude zero for the own-belief and cover-up contrasts against the Irrelevant Dialogue, reach essentially to zero for hidden factors against the Irrelevant Dialogue (upper limit -0.03), and include zero for the two significant contrasts against the Information List (own belief and hidden factors). Those two Experiment 1 results are therefore robust to worst-case attrition in point identification but are estimated with less precision once the trimmed comparison is bootstrapped. The Experiment 2 conclusions are unchanged when the 34 event-denial dialogues described in SM11 are excluded (Table SM11.2).

SM10. Selection into the follow-up surveys

Table SM10.1 reports the share of conspiracy believers in each condition of the initial experiment who returned for the follow-up survey. In Experiment 2, return was slightly higher in the Debunking Dialogue condition (85.7%) than in the pooled control conditions (81.6%), p = .095 (p = .096 when the 34 eventdenial dialogues described in SM11 are excluded). The preregistration (AsPredicted #251092) called for Lee bounds on the follow-up outcomes if return rates differed significantly; because the difference, although not significant, is not negligible, we report those bounds below (Table SM10.4). In Experiment 1 the return rates were nearly identical (58.7% vs. 58.1%, p = .98).

If the treated participants who showed the largest immediate belief change were the ones who came back, the returning treated sample would be enriched for responders, and every follow-up estimate would be biased toward finding carry-over. To test this directly, we regressed each observed post-treatment outcome (without imputing dropouts; believer sample of the main experiment) on a Debunking Dialogue dummy, an indicator for returning to the follow-up, their interaction, and the mean-centered pre-treatment value of the same outcome, with HC2 robust standard errors. A negative interaction on the three conspiracy-belief outcomes (a positive one for trust) indicates that the returned-minus-not-returned gap in post-treatment belief was more favorable to the treatment among treated participants than among controls, i.e., the selection pattern of concern. Table SM10.2 reports the interaction and the returned-minus-not-returned difference estimated separately within each condition. For Experiment 2 we also test the three-item post-treatment Kirk composite, which is the t 1 measure of the persistence analysis (SM12).

Of the eight interaction tests, one is significant. On the Experiment 2 cover-up item, treated returnees scored 3.05 points lower than treated non-returners (p = .14), whereas control returnees scored 1.95 points higher than control non-returners (p = .042), for an interaction of -5.22 (95% CI [-9.68, -0.77], p = .022).

No such pattern appears on the primary outcome (participants' own conspiracy belief; b = -2.14, p = .43: treated returnees rated their belief 2.30 points lower than treated non-returners, p = .32, and control returnees 0.01 points lower than control non-returners, p = .99), on hidden factors or trust, on the three-item composite that enters the persistence analysis (b = -2.72, p = .153), or on any Experiment 1 outcome (all p ≥ .060; the smallest p-value is for trust in the official explanation). The immediate treatment effect on participants' own belief (Debunking Dialogue versus the pooled controls, adjusting for the pre-treatment rating) is -7.54 points among returnees (n = 851), -6.40 among non-returners (n = 166), and -7.21 among all believers with an observed post-treatment score (n = 1,017); for the three-item composite the corresponding estimates are -6.36, -3.63, and -5.94. In Experiment 1 the corresponding estimates for participants' own belief are -9.13 points among returnees (n = 270), -4.63 among non-returners (n = 165), and -7.45 among all believers with an observed post-treatment score (n = 435); the return × condition interaction is in the direction of concern but not significant (b = -4.51, p = .135).

To account for possible selective return in the follow-up estimates themselves, we re-estimated every follow-up analysis with each returning participant weighted by the inverse of their estimated probability of returning. The probability of returning was estimated by logistic regression, fit separately within the Debunking Dialogue condition and within the pooled control conditions among all conspiracy believers randomized in the experiment (N = 1,042 in Experiment 2; N = 462 in Experiment 1), on the four pretreatment ratings (own belief, cover-up, hidden factors, trust in the official explanation), the four post-treatment ratings of the same items (with the pre-treatment value carried forward for participants who quit before the post-treatment measures, as in the main analyses), age, education, party identification, belief in God, and trust in AI. Weighting the returnees in this way makes them resemble the full randomized sample on these characteristics: the largest standardized difference between returnees and all randomized believers of the same condition on any of the 13 covariates falls from .07 to .01 in Experiment 2 and from .11 to .03 in Experiment 1. The weights are moderate (1.01 to 2.15 in Experiment 2; 1.03 to 3.32 in Experiment 1), so little precision is lost (effective sample sizes of 862 of 872 and 256 of 270 returnees). The weighted models are otherwise identical to the unweighted ones. Standard errors are heteroskedasticity-robust and treat the weights as fixed; a bootstrap that re-estimates the weights in each of 2,000 resamples gives very similar intervals, and supplies the intervals for the indirect effects.

Table SM10.3 compares the weighted and unweighted estimates. In Experiment 1, the effects of the Debunking Dialogue on the follow-up outcomes are essentially unchanged by weighting (odds ratios of .55, .47, and .49; all p ≤ .023). In Experiment 2, the estimate for LDS conspiracy belief remains near zero (b = -0.03, p = .98), and the persistence slopes and the indirect effects through immediate belief change are essentially unchanged. The estimate for generic conspiracy beliefs, however, is smaller after weighting and no longer significant (b = -2.34, 95% CI [-5.61, 0.92], p = .16, compared with b = -3.33, p = .044, unweighted). The same pattern holds when the weights are truncated at their 99th percentile (b = -2.44, p = .14), when the return model includes only the eight belief ratings (b = -2.88, p = .083), and when it adds an indicator for having completed the post-treatment measures (b = -2.32, p = .16).

Two limitations apply. First, weighting corrects only for selection on the measured characteristics; it cannot correct for return that depends on unmeasured factors or on the follow-up beliefs themselves. Second, in Experiment 1 none of the 27 believers who quit before the post-treatment measures (24 in the Debunking

Excluding the 34 flagged dialogues changes no coefficient by more than 0.12 points on the 0-100 scale: the seven contrasts that are significant in the main text remain significant at p < .001, and trust in the official explanation versus the Information List remains non-significant (p = .17 vs. p = .16). The Lee bounds are likewise unchanged in every respect; the identified sets and outer intervals of all seven significant contrasts exclude zero. mediation model that combines the two preregistered analyses. With t 1 the post-treatment Kirk composite and t 0 the pre-treatment composite, the a-path model is t 1 ∼ DD + t 0 , the b-path model is y ∼ DD + t 1 + t 0 (whose DD coefficient is the direct effect), and the total-effect model is y ∼ DD + t 0 ; the indirect effect is a × b, with a percentile bootstrap 95% CI (5,000 resamples). In the ITT cohort (n = 851 returnees with t 0 , t 1 , and the follow-up outcome observed), assignment to the Debunking Dialogue lowered the post-treatment composite by 6.36 points ([-8.10, -4.62]), and the post-treatment composite predicted both follow-up outcomes given assignment and baseline (b = .182, p = .005, for generic conspiracy beliefs; b = .123, p = .038, for LDS shooting beliefs). The indirect effects are -1.16 points (95% bootstrap CI [-2.11, -0.33]) on generic conspiracy beliefs and -0.78 points ([-1.54, -0.07]) on LDS shooting beliefs; the direct effects are -1.33 (p = .39) and +0.61 (p = .66), and the total effects -2.49 (p = .10) and -0.17 (p = .90), estimated on the 851 rows with an observed t 1 and therefore slightly different from the 872-row ANCOVAs of Table SM12.1. The per-protocol cohort gives indirect effects of -1.18 ([-2.06, -0.34]) and -0.79 ([-1.51, -0.04]). The indirect effect is the immediate treatment effect scaled by the persistence slope: the a-path is experimental, but the b-path is not, so the indirect effect is identified under sequential ignorability-no unmeasured confounding of the relation between post-treatment belief and follow-up belief, given assignment and t 0 -which is the same assumption as the persistence analysis, and it shares its observational character.

Table SM10.4 reports Lee bounds (computed as in SM9) for the two Experiment 2 follow-up outcomes, treating return to the follow-up as the response and comparing the Debunking Dialogue condition with the pooled control conditions and with each control condition separately. Because the Debunking Dialogue condition was better retained, 4.7% of its returnees are trimmed in the pooled comparison. For generic conspiracy beliefs the identified set lies below zero ([-5.72, -1.06]), but the bootstrap outer 95% confidence interval, which also reflects sampling uncertainty, includes zero ([-9.66, 3.01]); for LDS conspiracy belief both the identified set ([-2.53, 1.64]) and the outer interval ([-5.95, 5.15]) include zero. The bounds are computed on unadjusted follow-up means.

SM11. Dialogues that denied the event, and analyses excluding them

In Experiment 2 the dialogue model, whose training data predate the event, occasionally asserted during a Debunking Dialogue that Charlie Kirk had not in fact been killed. Blind LLM coding of all Debunking Dialogue transcripts flagged 37 such dialogues. Three of the 37 participants had already been removed by the pre-randomization survey-agent screen (a hidden instruction designed to detect automated respondents). The remaining 34 completed the post-treatment measures. Excluding them would be a post-randomization exclusion that can only remove participants from the dialogue condition, so every analysis of treatment effects in the main text retains them in their assigned condition (intention-to-treat). Of the 34, the GPT-4o belief classification (SM3) coded 27 as "no," 6 as "maybe," and 1 as "yes"; since the main analyses are restricted to participants classified as "yes" or "maybe," 7 of the 34 are in the believer sample (N = 1,042).

As a sensitivity analysis, Table SM11.1 sets the eight pairwise immediate-effect contrasts of the main text beside the same contrasts estimated after excluding the 34 dialogues (the per-protocol sample; N = 1,035 believers), and Table SM11.2 repeats the Lee bounds of SM9 on that sample. The follow-up analyses likewise retain everyone (N = 872 returning believers, including the six whose dialogues were flagged); SM12 reports the follow-up cohort without them (N = 866) for comparison.

SM12. Experiment 2 follow-up: cohort, covariates, persistence, and mediation

The follow-up analyses use the intention-to-treat (ITT) follow-up cohort, as in the main text: every believer in the main-experiment sample who returned to the follow-up survey, N = 872 (454 Debunking Dialogue / 211 Information List / 207 Irrelevant Dialogue). Table SM12.1 also reports the per-protocol follow-up cohort, which excludes the six returning believers whose dialogues denied the event (SM11; N = 866; 448 / 211 / 207), for comparison; across the two cohorts no estimate differs by more than 0.2 points on the 0-100 scale and no persistence slope by more than .01.
